definition: Longer range than 5 GHz, better wall penetration. More congested (shared with Bluetooth, microwaves, baby monitors, neighbors' networks). Only 3 non-overlapping 20MHz channels: 1, 6, and 11 in North America. Slower maximum throughput than 5 GHz. Best for: devices far from AP, environments requiring maximum range.

3 copies of data. 2 different storage media types (e.g., local disk + NAS, or NAS + tape). 1 copy offsite (cloud, remote facility, physical tape offsite rotation). Protects against: single device failure (3 copies), media-specific failure like disk firmware bug (2 media types), site disaster like fire or flood (1 offsite). Industry-standard best practice.
Hard architectural cap at 4 GB RAM regardless of physical RAM installed. Can only run 32-bit OS and 32-bit applications.

64-bit Windows runs both 32-bit and 64-bit apps. 32-bit (x86) Windows CANNOT run 64-bit applications — period. On 64-bit Windows: 64-bit apps install to C:\Program Files. 32-bit apps install to C:\Program Files (x86). The (x86) folder exists because 32-bit apps use different system libraries — separation prevents conflicts. WOW64 subsystem enables 32-bit apps on 64-bit OS.

Additive manufacturing — builds objects layer by layer. FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling): heats and extrudes thermoplastic filament (PLA, ABS, PETG) through nozzle onto build plate. Bed leveling: critical — uneven bed causes print adhesion failures. Extruder calibration: correct filament flow rate. SLA (Stereolithography): UV laser cures liquid resin layer by layer — higher resolution than FDM. SLS (Selective Laser Sintering): laser sinters powdered material — used for industrial/engineering parts.

Print not adhering to bed: bed not level (re-level), bed temperature wrong (PLA=60°C, ABS=100°C), first layer too high (lower Z offset). Stringing (fine threads between parts): print temperature too high, retraction settings incorrect. Layer separation: print temperature too low, cooling too aggressive. Clogged nozzle: cold pull cleaning or replace nozzle.

Shorter range, less wall penetration. Much less congested — 23+ non-overlapping 20 MHz channels in North America. Faster throughput. Best for: devices near AP, high-density environments, video streaming.

Newest. Available only in Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices. 1200 MHz of spectrum — over 14 non-overlapping 80 MHz channels. Very low congestion (no legacy device interference). Very short range. Wi-Fi 6E devices and APs required for 6 GHz connectivity.

Supports up to 2 TB RAM (Pro) or 6 TB (Enterprise/Pro for Workstations). Runs 32-bit apps via WOW64 (Windows 32-bit on Windows 64-bit) compatibility layer. 32-bit apps install to Program Files (x86) — 64-bit apps install to Program Files. 64-bit CANNOT run on 32-bit hardware.

80 Plus: 80% efficiency at 20%, 50%, and 100% load (standard 115V testing). Higher tiers: Bronze (85%), Silver (88%), Gold (92%), Platinum (94%), Titanium (96%). Higher efficiency = less wasted heat = lower electricity cost. Gold is generally the sweet spot for consumer builds.

802.11a: 5 GHz, 54 Mbps (legacy, 1999). 802.11b: 2.4 GHz, 11 Mbps (legacy, 1999). 802.11g: 2.4 GHz, 54 Mbps (legacy, 2003). 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4): dual-band 2.4+5 GHz, up to 600 Mbps, MIMO (2009). 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5): 5 GHz only, up to 3.5 Gbps, MU-MIMO, 80/160 MHz channels (2013). 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6): 2.4+5 GHz, up to 9.6 Gbps, OFDMA, TWT, BSS Coloring (2019). Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz band. Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be): multi-link operation, 30+ Gbps.

Three-party model: Supplicant (client), Authenticator (AP or switch), Authentication Server (RADIUS). Supplicant sends credentials to Authenticator → forwards to Auth Server → Accept/Reject → port opened or blocked. Used for wireless Enterprise and wired switch port access control.

Organizations increasingly add AI-specific AUP provisions: prohibit entering PII/PHI/confidential data into public AI tools, define approved vs unapproved AI tools, require human review of AI output before use in official capacity, address copyright and attribution requirements for AI-generated work.

Double-door airlock entry system. First door must fully close and lock before the second door can open. PREVENTS TAILGATING — an unauthorized person cannot follow through before the door closes. This is the most effective physical control against tailgating. Required at data center entrances and high-security areas.

Three methods: (1) Settings > System > Recovery > Advanced Startup > Restart Now. (2) Shift+Restart from login screen or Start menu. (3) Boot from Windows installation media (USB/DVD) > Repair your computer. After 2–3 failed boots, Windows automatically enters WinRE. F8 at boot works on some older systems but is unreliable on Windows 10/11 with fast startup.
Active Directory: set expiration date for contractor/temp accounts. Auto-disables after date — critical for contractor lifecycle management.
Threshold (attempts before lockout), Duration (minutes locked), Observation window (time to reset counter). Prevents brute force. Too aggressive = inadvertent denial of service.

OUs: containers for GPO application. ADUC manages user accounts. Disable (don't delete) departing employee accounts. Security groups: assign resource permissions to group (never individual users at scale). Login scripts run at domain logon. Home folders use %username% variable in path. Folder Redirection (GPO): moves Desktop/Documents to network share — user sees local path, data on server.
macOS equivalent of Windows Task Manager. Shows real-time CPU, memory, disk, network, energy usage by process. Identify resource-heavy apps. Located: /Applications/Utilities.

HDMI-to-VGA: active adapter required (digital to analog conversion). DisplayPort-to-HDMI: often passive (DP can natively output HDMI signal). USB-C-to-HDMI/DP: uses Alt Mode — passive for DP, active for HDMI in some cases. DVI-to-HDMI: passive (both digital, compatible signals). DVI-to-VGA: active adapter (DVI-A or DVI-I only — DVI-D digital cannot convert to analog passively).

G-Sync (NVIDIA proprietary): requires G-Sync hardware module in monitor. More expensive. Better compatibility. FreeSync (AMD, open standard): uses VESA Adaptive Sync. Less expensive. Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) in general. Eliminates screen tearing (occurs when GPU frame rate and monitor refresh rate are mismatched) and reduces stutter. VRR range: e.g., 48–144 Hz.
Displays unwanted ads in browsers. Often bundled with free software. Categorized as PUP. Degrades performance.
The strong cipher for WPA2/WPA3. Advanced Encryption Standard with 128/192/256-bit keys. No practical attack. Always use this cipher.

Broad field of computer science focused on creating systems that perform tasks that normally require human intelligence: reasoning, problem-solving, learning, understanding language, recognizing patterns. AI is the umbrella term — machine learning and generative AI are subfields.

AI models sometimes generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information with apparent confidence. Called "hallucination." Causes: gaps in training data, pattern completion without true understanding, no real-time fact verification. Critical rule: always verify AI output against authoritative sources before acting on it in a professional context, especially for technical procedures, commands, and configurations.

IT technicians encounter AI tools for: automated troubleshooting suggestions, chatbot first-line support, script generation, log analysis and anomaly detection, documentation generation, patch management prioritization. Understanding AI capabilities and limitations is now part of the A+ exam scope.

Heatsink: metal block (aluminum base, copper/aluminum fins) with high surface area. Attaches directly over CPU with mounting brackets. Fan mounted on heatsink blows air through fins. Requires thermal paste between CPU and heatsink base for heat transfer. Must be compatible with CPU socket. Tower cooler: fins and fan oriented for better airflow through case (larger, more efficient than low-profile).

Disables ALL radios: cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS/NFC. Required during flight (regulations). After enabling, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can be individually re-enabled (for in-flight entertainment systems, wireless headphones). GPS can also be re-enabled (receive-only, no transmission).

Omni-directional: radiates equally in all directions (360° horizontal). Standard for general-purpose coverage. Dipole antennas on APs. Directional: focuses signal in one direction — longer range in that direction. Types: Yagi, parabolic dish, panel antenna. Used for: point-to-point links, long-distance outdoor wireless bridges.

Metallic-looking Faraday cage bags that protect components from ESD during transport and storage. Conductive exterior, insulating interior — electric field is dissipated across the outer surface. Never place components on top of antistatic bag — only inside.

Worn on wrist, connected to chassis ground or grounding point via a resistor (1 megaohm — allows static to drain slowly, protecting both technician and equipment). Never connect directly to mains ground (shock hazard). Must contact skin. Do not wear near CRTs or high-voltage equipment.

Apple File System — macOS, iOS, iPadOS default since 2018. Optimized for SSDs. Native encryption and snapshot support. Multiple volumes share one physical storage pool. Not compatible with non-Apple operating systems.

Automatic Private IP Addressing. If Windows cannot contact a DHCP server, it self-assigns an address in 169.254.0.0/16 range. A 169.254.x.x address = DHCP failure. Run ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew to force DHCP renegotiation.

169.254.0.0/16 range. Windows self-assigns address in this range when DHCP server is unreachable. Devices with APIPA can communicate with other APIPA devices on the same segment but CANNOT reach the internet or communicate with normally-addressed devices. Symptom: 169.254.x.x address = DHCP failure — check DHCP server, cable/connectivity, DHCP scope exhaustion.

Self-assigned when DHCP server unreachable. Cannot communicate with internet or normal-address devices. Causes: DHCP server down, DHCP scope exhausted (all addresses in use), network connectivity issue preventing DHCP Discover from reaching server. Fix: verify DHCP server running, check DHCP scope has available addresses, check network path from client to DHCP server. Temporary fix: assign static IP.

See Core 2 section 3.4 for complete app troubleshooting sequence: Force stop → Clear cache → Clear data → Reinstall → Update OS. Low storage = app crashes and update failures. Close background apps if RAM is low (though modern iOS/Android manage this automatically).

Standard escalation path: (1) Force stop the app (Settings > Apps > [App] > Force Stop). (2) Clear app cache (Settings > Apps > [App] > Storage > Clear Cache) — removes temporary files without deleting user data. (3) Clear app data (Settings > Apps > [App] > Storage > Clear Data) — resets app to factory defaults, deletes all local data and settings. (4) Uninstall and reinstall the app. (5) Update the app (or OS). (6) Factory reset as last resort.

Causes: insufficient storage, app store account issue, network connectivity, device compatibility with new version. Fix: check storage, sign out and back into app store account, clear app store cache, check if device OS version meets new app requirements.

Application stops responding: Task Manager > Processes > right-click > End Task. DLL errors: missing or wrong version DLL — reinstall application or install Visual C++ redistributable. Application compatibility: right-click > Properties > Compatibility tab — run in compatibility mode for older Windows versions. 32-bit app on 64-bit OS: supported via WOW64, installs to Program Files (x86).

Use Settings > Apps > Apps and Features or Control Panel > Programs and Features — NEVER delete application folders directly (leaves registry entries and user data, causes reinstall issues). Repair mode: most installers support repair — reinstalls files without removing user settings.

Compatibility mode: right-click app > Properties > Compatibility tab > run in compatibility mode for older Windows version. Run as administrator: for apps needing elevated rights to function. Repair installation: most installers support repair mode — reinstalls files without removing user data. Uninstall/reinstall as last resort. Check Event Viewer > Application log for crash-time errors.
Fake ARP replies associate attacker's MAC with legitimate IP (usually default gateway). Traffic destined for gateway goes to attacker instead. Enables MITM on local network.

Tracks all IT assets: hardware (serial numbers, purchase dates, warranty expiry, location, assigned user), software (licenses, versions, install dates). Enables: license compliance audits, hardware refresh planning, theft/loss detection, warranty claims. Can be a spreadsheet, CMDB, or dedicated tool. Each asset gets an asset tag (barcode/QR code label).
Drive firmware command erasing ALL flash cells including wear-leveled cells. The controller reaches all physical cells — software overwrite tools cannot. Recommended method for SSDs.

Attended: technician physically present, responds to setup prompts (appropriate for single machines). Unattended: uses a preconfigured answer file (unattend.xml or autounattend.xml) containing all responses — no human present after start. Foundation of enterprise deployment at scale.

No sound from speaker: check volume (both media volume and ring volume), check DND/silent mode, check if Bluetooth device is connected and routing audio. Speaker test: call someone. If call audio works but media doesn't = software/volume setting. If neither = hardware.

Internal organizational policy defining permitted and prohibited use of company IT resources: computers, network, email, internet. Common prohibitions: personal use (depends on company), accessing adult/illegal content, sharing credentials, installing unauthorized software, using company systems for personal business. Employees typically sign AUP at hire. Violations are grounds for disciplinary action.

AAA: Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what can you do?), Accounting (what did you do?). RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service): port 1812 (auth), 1813 (accounting). Central authentication for network access — VPN, Wi-Fi (WPA2-Enterprise), 802.1X wired. TACACS+ (Cisco): port 49, TCP, encrypts entire packet (vs RADIUS which only encrypts password). Used for network device admin authentication (switches, routers).

Automatic Medium-Dependent Interface Crossover. Modern switches automatically detect and correct cable type — a straight-through works where crossover was previously required. Enabled by default on most modern equipment. When auto-MDIX is disabled or on legacy equipment, correct cable type matters.

term: Azure AD Connect / Microsoft Entra Connect
definition: Installed on-premises Windows Server. Synchronizes on-premises Active Directory users/groups/attributes to Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). Default sync interval: 30 minutes. After sync: users can use on-premises credentials for Microsoft 365 — hybrid identity. Password sync options: Password Hash Sync (hash synced to cloud), Pass-through Authentication (auth requests forwarded to on-prem DC), Federation with ADFS.

LED backlight (standard in all modern laptops): efficient, thin, long lifespan. Edge-lit (LEDs around the perimeter, light guide distributes across panel) vs FALD (Full Array Local Dimming — LEDs behind entire panel in zones, better contrast). CCFL backlight (legacy, pre-2010): fluorescent tubes behind panel, thicker, heavier, contains mercury — requires special disposal. CCFLs and LEDs are NOT interchangeable as replacement parts.

Local disk: fast, convenient, single point of failure. NAS (Network Attached Storage): shared network backup target, fast, still on-premises. Tape: slow sequential access, high capacity, cheap long-term archival, offsite transport. Cloud: offsite by nature, scalable, recovery speed limited by internet bandwidth. Optical (Blu-ray/DVD): archival only, limited capacity.

In-place restore: restore to original location (same server/workstation). Alternate location restore: restore to different server or different path — used when original system unavailable or for testing. Bare metal restore: restore full system image to new/blank hardware — OS, applications, and data restored from single image. File/folder level restore: recover specific files without full system restore.

RFID proximity cards or magnetic stripe cards at access points. Logs who entered and when — creates an audit trail. Smart cards have embedded microprocessor chips and require insertion or tap against reader. Key fobs transmit wireless RFID signals to readers. Mobile digital keys use Bluetooth or NFC on a smartphone.

Basic disk: uses MBR or GPT, has primary/extended/logical partitions. Standard for all workstations. Dynamic disk: supports volume sets (spanning multiple disks), software RAID configurations (mirrored, striped). Managed through Disk Management. Converting basic to dynamic is non-destructive; dynamic to basic requires deleting all volumes.

Li-ion (Lithium-ion) chemistry. Rated in mAh (milliamp-hours) or Wh (watt-hours) — higher = more capacity = longer runtime. Degrades over charge cycles (~300–500 full cycles before noticeable capacity loss. Swollen/puffed battery: gas buildup inside the cell — fire/explosion hazard. Immediate action: stop charging, do not puncture, remove if safe (laptop may need to be opened), proper hazardous disposal. Never use a swollen battery.

Battery drains quickly: check Settings > Battery > Battery Usage — identify high-consumption apps. Disable background refresh, location services, push email. Screen brightness. Poor cellular signal (device boosts transmit power). Old/degraded battery (replace). Device won't charge: try different cable, different charger, clean charging port (lint compacted in USB-C/Lightning port — use toothpick carefully). Wireless charging: alignment matters — reposition device. Charging but won't charge above X%: battery health issue.

All rechargeable batteries (Li-ion, NiMH, NiCd) are hazardous waste — must NOT go in regular trash. Lead-acid batteries (UPS) are also regulated. Many electronics retailers accept battery drop-off. Call2Recycle is a common US battery recycling program. Single-use alkaline batteries: regulations vary by state (some allow regular trash, some require recycling).

Causes: background apps running with location/sync services active, screen brightness too high, outdated battery (Li-ion degrades over ~300–500 full charge cycles), resource-intensive apps, poor cellular signal (device increases transmit power searching for signal). Diagnosis: Settings > Battery > Battery Usage shows per-app consumption. Fix: reduce brightness, disable background app refresh, enable low-power mode, replace battery if capacity has degraded.

POST beep codes vary by BIOS manufacturer. AMI BIOS: 1 short = POST success. 2 short = POST error. 3 long = RAM not detected. 1 long + 2 short = GPU error. Award BIOS: 1 long + 2 short = display adapter error. Phoenix BIOS: triplet codes (1-1-3 = CMOS failure). Refer to motherboard documentation for specific manufacturer. No speaker connected or speaker failed = no beep codes heard — add PC speaker to front panel header to test.

Fingerprint reader: USB or I2C connected, built into power button or palmrest. Supports Windows Hello sign-in. IR camera (see Webcam above): supports Windows Hello facial recognition via Near Infrared (NIR) imaging — works even in total darkness.

Fingerprint scanners: most common, reads ridge patterns — on laptops, phones, doors. Retina scanner: analyzes blood vessel pattern on back of eye, extremely accurate, considered invasive (eye must be close to scanner). Facial recognition: maps facial features via camera, varies in security level (2D = defeatable by photo; 3D infrared like Face ID = highly accurate). Voice recognition: analyzes speech patterns. Palm print scanner: reads entire palm surface pattern.

BIOS (Basic Input/Output System): legacy 16-bit firmware. Text-only interface. Supports MBR partition table only. 2.2 TB maximum drive size. No Secure Boot or GPT support. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface): modern replacement. GUI interface with mouse support. Supports GPT partition table (required for drives >2.2 TB). Secure Boot support. Fast boot options. Network support pre-OS. UEFI with CSM (Compatibility Support Module) can still boot legacy OS.
Supervisor password: highest privilege, controls all BIOS settings. User password: required to boot, limited BIOS access. Both prevent boot order changes (USB booting to bypass OS).

Boot order: priority of devices to boot from (USB, NVME, optical). XMP (Intel) / EXPO (AMD): profiles for RAM to run at rated speed above JEDEC spec — enable in BIOS to use purchased RAM at advertised speed. Virtualization: VT-x (Intel) / AMD-V (AMD) — must enable for hypervisors. Secure Boot: verifies boot loader cryptographic signature — required for Windows 11. TPM (Trusted Platform Module): security chip for BitLocker, Windows Hello, Windows 11 requirement. Fan control: configure fan curves for cooling vs noise balance.

Full volume encryption on Windows Pro/Enterprise/Education. Requires TPM 1.2 or higher (TPM 2.0 preferred). TPM stores encryption keys and verifies system integrity during boot. If no TPM: can use USB startup key. Recovery: 48-digit numeric recovery key (must be saved to AD, USB, printed, or Microsoft account before enabling). BitLocker protects drive if physically removed from machine — drive is unreadable without key. Manages via Control Panel > BitLocker Drive Encryption or manage-bde command.

BitLocker: volume-level, protects entire drive including OS, requires TPM, protects against physical theft of drive. EFS: file-level, NTFS only, tied to user certificate, protects individual files from other users on same machine. They can be used together.

BitLocker applied to removable drives (USB flash, external HDD). Right-click drive → Turn on BitLocker. Unlocked with password or smart card. Readable on other Windows machines with correct password. Protects removable media if lost or stolen.

Short-range wireless PAN (Personal Area Network). Range: ~10 meters (Class 2). Version 5.0+: up to 40m range, 2 Mbps, improved coexistence with Wi-Fi. Uses 2.4 GHz ISM band. Pairing: discoverable mode → PIN or passkey match → bonded (remembered). Profiles determine capabilities: A2DP (audio streaming), HFP (hands-free calls), HID (keyboard/mouse), PBAP (phone book access). Auto-connect to bonded devices.

Bluejacking: sending unsolicited messages/contacts to a nearby Bluetooth device. Nuisance, not data theft. Bluesnarfing: unauthorized access to data (contacts, calendar, messages) on a Bluetooth-enabled device by exploiting Bluetooth vulnerabilities. More serious than bluejacking. Bluebugging: taking full control of a Bluetooth device. Prevention: keep Bluetooth off when not in use, do not pair with unknown devices, keep device firmware updated.

Heavy reinforced posts (concrete or steel) positioned at building entrances. Prevent vehicle-borne attacks — stop a vehicle from ramming through a wall or door. Used at building perimeters and critical facility entrances.
Dual-boot Windows on Intel Macs. Deprecated on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) — not supported on ARM-based Macs. Installs Windows drivers for Apple hardware.

"BOOTMGR is missing": missing/corrupt boot manager file — run bootrec /fixmbr then /fixboot. "No OS found" / "Operating System not found": BIOS cannot find bootable device — check boot order in BIOS, check drive connection, check if drive failed. "Inaccessible Boot Device": Windows cannot access the partition — may be missing driver for storage controller, corrupt partition table, or wrong partition set as active.

USB flash drive/external drive: most common modern method — write ISO using Media Creation Tool, set BIOS/UEFI boot order to USB first. Optical disc (DVD/Blu-ray): legacy but exam-relevant. PXE (Preboot Execution Environment): network boot — machine reaches DHCP server, gets IP + boot server location, downloads boot image. PXE REQUIRES DHCP — without it, the machine cannot find the boot server. Internal recovery partition: OEM hidden partition with factory image (F11 or Ctrl+F11 at startup) — LOST if the drive is replaced. Internet-based: macOS Recovery Mode (Cmd+R) downloads and reinstalls macOS from Apple servers.

bootrec /fixmbr — rewrites the Master Boot Record without touching the partition table. bootrec /fixboot — writes a new boot sector to the active partition. bootrec /scanos — scans all disks for Windows installations. bootrec /rebuildbcd — scans all disks and rebuilds the Boot Configuration Data (BCD) store — most commonly needed. "BOOTMGR is missing" = run bootrec /fixmbr then bootrec /rebuildbcd.

"Boot device not found," "No bootable media," "Operating system not found." Causes: boot order wrong (check BIOS — make sure correct drive first), drive failed, MBR/GPT/BCD corrupted (run bootrec from WinRE), loose SATA cable. Fix boot order in BIOS first (simplest). If drive present but won't boot: WinRE Startup Repair or bootrec commands.

bootrec /fixmbr: writes new Master Boot Record — use when MBR is corrupt (boot sector virus, failed disk op). bootrec /fixboot: writes new boot sector to active partition — use when BOOTMGR is missing after fixing MBR. bootrec /rebuildbcd: scans all drives for Windows installations and rebuilds Boot Configuration Data — use when Windows exists but is not in boot menu. bootrec /scanos: scans for Windows installations without rebuilding BCD. Run all three in sequence: /fixmbr → /fixboot → /rebuildbcd, then reboot.
Network of compromised machines controlled via C2 server. Used for DDoS, spam, credential stuffing, cryptomining.

Homepage changes without user action. Search engine redirected to unfamiliar site. New toolbars or extensions appear. Popups and ads appear on normally clean sites. Cause: PUP (Potentially Unwanted Program) or browser hijacker installed via bundled software or malicious download. Fix: remove suspicious extensions, reset browser settings, run malware scan, check installed programs.
Keep browser updated — browser vulnerabilities actively exploited. Extensions: official stores ONLY (Chrome Web Store, Firefox Add-ons, Edge Add-ons). Review permissions. Remove unused. Keep updated.
Systematically tries all password combinations. Mitigated by lockout policy, CAPTCHA, MFA.

Also called Stop Error or Stop Screen. Windows halts completely when it detects a fatal system error that cannot be safely recovered. Displays a stop code (e.g., IRQLNOTLESSOREQUAL), a QR code, and collects a memory dump. Modern Windows 10/11 BSODs show a sad face and a stop code. After crash, Windows attempts automatic restart.

Immediate action: power off and unplug. Identify source before powering on again. Causes: short circuit, failed component, overloaded circuit. Inspect motherboard, PSU, and cables for visible damage. Burning smell from PSU = PSU failure (replace immediately).
Employee-owned device for work. Policy must address: data ownership, MDM enrollment requirements, acceptable use, remote wipe consent. Containerization separates corporate/personal data.

Group of stakeholders (IT management, system owners, security, business representatives) that reviews and approves normal changes. Reviews: change description, impact analysis, rollback plan, maintenance window, risk assessment. CAB meeting typically weekly or bi-weekly. Emergency changes bypass CAB but undergo retroactive review.
Steel cable and anchor lock securing laptops and monitors to fixed surfaces. Named after the Kensington security standard (K-Slot on laptops). Prevents opportunistic theft of portable equipment.

Route cables to avoid trip hazards — use cable covers or run under floors/ceilings. Secure cables with cable ties (not zip ties pulled so tight they pinch cables). Label cables at both ends. Keep power cables separated from data cables to reduce EMI.

Cable modem: connects to cable TV infrastructure (DOCSIS standard). Coaxial cable to ISP. DSL modem: connects over telephone copper pair. Types: ADSL (asymmetric — faster download than upload), VDSL (faster, shorter distance). ONT (Optical Network Terminal): fiber-to-premises termination device — converts optical signal to Ethernet.

Verifies physical cable wiring. Detects: opens (broken conductor), shorts (conductors touching), reversed pairs, split pairs, incorrect termination standard (T568A vs T568B). Basic tester: sends signal through each pin, verifies continuity. Advanced (certifier): measures attenuation, crosstalk, confirms cable meets CAT spec.

SRAM (Static RAM) — faster and more expensive than DRAM. Built into CPU die. L1 cache: smallest (32–64 KB per core), fastest, accessed first. L2 cache: larger (256 KB – 1 MB per core), slightly slower. L3 cache: largest (8–32+ MB, shared across all cores), slowest of the caches but still much faster than RAM. Reduces CPU wait time for frequently accessed data.

Cache: temporary files used to speed up app performance — safe to clear, will rebuild. Data: user settings, saved preferences, login credentials, local database — clearing this resets the app completely (user must log in again, settings lost). Always try clear cache before clear data.

Electrolytic capacitors on motherboard can fail — visible symptoms: tops of capacitors are domed/bulging (normally flat) or have brownish residue leak. Symptoms: system instability, random crashes, BSOD, boot failures. Capacitors cannot be repaired by end user — motherboard replacement required.

Positive pressure: more intake fans than exhaust fans — slightly higher internal pressure, reduces dust ingress through unfiltered gaps (but requires more filtered intakes). Negative pressure: more exhaust than intake — cooler ambient air drawn in through gaps, more dust accumulation. Neutral pressure: balanced intake and exhaust — most common recommendation. Airflow path: cool air in (front/bottom) → flows over components → hot air out (rear/top). Keep cable management tidy — bundled cables block airflow.

CAT5: 100 Mbps (Fast Ethernet), 100m max. Largely obsolete. CAT5e (e=enhanced): 1 Gbps (Gigabit Ethernet), 100m. Eliminates near-end crosstalk. Current minimum standard. CAT6: 1 Gbps at 100m, 10 Gbps at 55m. Tighter twists, larger diameter than CAT5e. CAT6a (a=augmented): 10 Gbps at 100m. Thicker, heavier, often shielded. Required for full-distance 10GbE. CAT7: shielded, 10 Gbps+, 100m, uses GG45 or TERA connectors (not RJ-45 — rarely used). CAT8: 25/40 Gbps, 30m, data center use only.

Distributed network of edge servers geographically close to end users. Caches static content (images, video, CSS, JS). When user requests content: served from nearest edge server instead of origin server — lower latency, faster load time. Examples: Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS CloudFront. Reduces origin server load and improves global performance.

4G LTE: current standard, 100 Mbps average real-world. 5G sub-6 GHz: improved capacity and speed (1 Gbps+), similar coverage to 4G. 5G mmWave (millimeter wave): extremely fast (10 Gbps+), very short range, poor building penetration — only in dense urban areas near towers. eSIM: virtual SIM card embedded in device — activate carrier plan digitally without physical SIM swap. Dual SIM: two simultaneous cellular connections (physical SIM + eSIM).
Trusted root CAs pre-installed in OS and browser. Malware may install rogue root CA — enabling HTTPS interception without browser warnings. Check certificate stores for unauthorized entries.
Document from vendor recording: device serial numbers/asset tags, destruction method, date/location, chain of custody. Required for HIPAA, PCI-DSS compliance. May be audited — not optional.
FIRST hardening step for ALL devices. Default credentials publicly documented. Rename built-in Administrator. Set strong unique passwords on all devices — routers, printers, switches, workstations.

Period during which no changes are permitted regardless of approval — typically during critical business periods (fiscal year-end, holiday shopping season, elections, major product launches). Any change during a freeze requires executive waiver.

term: Change one thing at a time
definition: When testing: change only one variable per test. Changing multiple things simultaneously makes it impossible to identify which change resolved the issue.

Required elements of a change request: description of change and its purpose, scope (what systems/users affected), impact analysis (what could go wrong), rollback plan (exact steps to undo if needed), test plan (how you will verify success), maintenance window (when it will be done), approval signatures (CAB and system owner).

Standard (pre-approved): routine, well-documented, low-risk changes that have been pre-authorized — e.g., adding RAM to a server following established procedure. No CAB review needed each time. Normal: significant change requiring full CAB review and approval — e.g., upgrading a database server OS. Emergency: urgent change to resolve a critical incident — bypasses normal CAB review but must be reviewed retroactively.

Co-channel interference: two APs on the same channel compete for airtime — performance degradation. Adjacent-channel interference: overlapping channels cause more severe interference than co-channel. Solution: use only channels 1, 6, or 11 on 2.4 GHz. Rogue AP: unauthorized AP on your network — detected by wireless intrusion detection, site survey. Evil twin: AP with same SSID as legitimate network to lure clients.

Silicon chip set coordinating CPU communication with RAM, PCIe, storage, USB, and other peripherals. Intel chipsets: Z-series (overclocking + full PCIe lanes), B-series (mainstream, limited OC), H-series (budget, no OC). AMD chipsets: X-series (full features + OC), B-series (mainstream), A-series (budget). Determines feature set available on the motherboard.

Check Disk — verifies and repairs file system errors and bad sectors. chkdsk alone = read-only report. chkdsk /f = fix file system errors. chkdsk /r = locate bad sectors and recover readable data (includes /f). Cannot run /f on system drive while Windows is running — schedules for next boot. Requires admin.

Check Disk — scans and repairs NTFS file system errors. Syntax: chkdsk C: /f /r. /f: fixes file system errors. /r: locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implies /f). Must schedule for system drive (runs before Windows loads on next reboot). Run when: frequent read errors, application crashes, "file system error" messages, after abrupt power loss.

Classless Inter-Domain Routing. /prefix = number of 1-bits in subnet mask. /24 = 255.255.255.0. /16 = 255.255.0.0. /8 = 255.0.0.0. /30 = 255.255.255.252 (4 addresses, 2 usable — point-to-point links). /32 = single host (255.255.255.255).
Doors with numeric keypad codes. No physical keys to duplicate. Codes can be changed remotely. Used in secure areas where access codes are shared only with authorized personnel.

Formats the target partition and deploys OS fresh. All data, apps, and settings on that partition are deleted. Required when: repurposing a machine, OS is too corrupted, migrating to new hardware, or zero-configuration-drift consistency is needed. Most reliable installation type — starts from a known state.
System date/time is consistently wrong after power off — resets to 2000 or 2002 on boot. Cause: dead CMOS battery (CR2032). Replace battery. Re-enter BIOS date/time.

Base clock: guaranteed sustained speed (GHz). Boost/Turbo clock: maximum speed when thermal/power headroom allows — sustained for short bursts. Base: 3.5 GHz, Boost: 5.0 GHz example. Overclocking: running CPU above rated speed. Requires: unlocked multiplier (Intel K-series, all Ryzen chips are unlocked), Z-series chipset (Intel), adequate cooling. Voids warranty, increases heat and power.

Benefits: OpEx instead of CapEx (pay monthly vs large upfront hardware purchase), rapid provisioning, geographic redundancy, no hardware maintenance, scalability. Drawbacks: ongoing subscription cost (can exceed hardware cost over time), internet dependency, data sovereignty concerns (where is data stored physically — GDPR implications), vendor lock-in, security shared responsibility.

On-demand self-service: provision resources without human interaction with provider. Broad network access: accessible over network from diverse client platforms. Resource pooling: multi-tenant — provider serves many customers from shared infrastructure. Rapid elasticity: scale resources up/down quickly (appear unlimited to user). Measured service: pay-per-use metering — only pay for what you consume.

Public cloud: infrastructure shared across multiple tenants, operated by third-party provider (AWS, Azure, GCP). Low upfront cost, high scalability, no hardware management. Private cloud: dedicated infrastructure for one organization. On-premises or hosted. Greater control, compliance, and security. Higher cost. Hybrid cloud: combination — private for sensitive/regulated workloads, public for scalable/burst workloads. Complexity of managing both. Community cloud: shared between organizations with common requirements (multiple government agencies, healthcare networks).

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): virtual machines, storage, networking. Provider manages physical hardware and hypervisor. Customer manages: OS, runtime, applications, data. Maximum control, maximum responsibility. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine. PaaS (Platform as a Service): runtime environment, middleware, databases. Provider manages: infrastructure + OS + runtime. Customer manages: application code and data only. Examples: Azure App Service, Heroku, Google App Engine. SaaS (Software as a Service): complete hosted application. Provider manages everything. Customer just uses the app. Examples: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Dropbox, Gmail.

Object storage: stores data as objects with metadata — not file system. Unlimited scale, accessible via HTTP/API. Examples: AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage. Used for: backups, static web content, media. File storage: network file shares in cloud — NAS equivalent. Examples: Azure Files, AWS EFS. Block storage: raw disk volumes attached to VMs — like a hard drive. Examples: AWS EBS, Azure Managed Disks.

Advanced asset management that tracks not just assets but their relationships and dependencies. Example: Server X hosts VM Y, VM Y runs Application Z, Application Z is used by Department W. Enables impact analysis: "If server X fails, what else is affected?" Used in change management to assess blast radius of proposed changes. Foundation of ITSM (IT Service Management / ITIL framework).

CR2032 coin cell battery (3V). Powers the CMOS chip that stores BIOS settings (date/time, boot order, hardware configuration) when main power is off. Dead CMOS battery symptoms: date/time resets on every power cycle, BIOS settings don't save, CMOS checksum error on boot. Replacement: remove old battery, insert new, re-enter BIOS settings.
Multiple users editing same document simultaneously with live updates. Version history maintained automatically for rollback. Available in Microsoft 365 Online apps and Google Workspace.

Center conductor surrounded by insulator, metallic shield, and outer jacket. RG-6: standard for cable TV, satellite, and DOCSIS internet (cable modem). 75 ohm impedance. F-type connector (threaded). RG-59: older, thinner, lower signal quality — legacy CCTV. BNC connector: push-and-twist locking, used in legacy coax networks (10BASE-2) and some AV/security.

Color gamut standards: sRGB (standard for web, covers ~72% of DCI-P3). DCI-P3 (cinema standard, wider gamut). Adobe RGB (photography, even wider). Coverage percentage: "100% sRGB" = full sRGB gamut. Color accuracy measured in Delta-E (ΔE): ΔE < 2 = professional-grade accuracy. Factory calibrated displays: come with calibration reports.

Color laser or inkjet misaligned colors: run color calibration/alignment from printer utility. Each CMYK toner/cartridge must be aligned. Color calibration prints test pattern and uses optical sensor (or user feedback) to align registration.

Four separate toner cartridges: CMYK. One pass or four-pass process: four-pass older — drum makes four revolutions (one per color). One-pass modern — four drums in line (faster). Color registration: alignment of all four toner layers — misregistration causes color fringing.
Both NTFS and Share apply when accessing over network. MOST RESTRICTIVE wins. Local access = NTFS only (share permissions irrelevant).

Batch: REM keyword (REM This is a comment) or :: prefix. PowerShell: # character (# This is a comment). Python: # character. Bash: # character. VBScript: single quote '. Comments are ignored by the interpreter — documentation within scripts.

IRQLNOTLESSOREQUAL — driver attempted to access protected memory at wrong interrupt level (usually bad driver or RAM). PAGEFAULTINNONPAGEDAREA — system tried to access memory that should be in RAM but was not (bad RAM, driver, or corrupted system file). CRITICALPROCESSDIED — essential Windows process terminated unexpectedly (often corrupted system files). SYSTEMSERVICEEXCEPTION — system call failed, often driver-related. KERNELSECURITYCHECK_FAILURE — data corruption or driver integrity violation.

User account creation (batch onboarding). Software deployment and installation automation. Log file parsing and alerting. Scheduled maintenance tasks (disk cleanup, backup triggers). System inventory collection. Configuration management (setting registry keys, firewall rules). File and folder permission management.

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run — runs for ALL users at logon. HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run — runs for current user at logon. HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce — runs once then deletes entry. Malware adds entries here for persistence. Inspect with regedit or Autoruns (Sysinternals tool — more comprehensive than msconfig).

The structured methodology for all troubleshooting scenarios. Must be applied in this order on the exam. Step 1: Identify the problem. Step 2: Establish a theory of probable cause. Step 3: Test the theory. Step 4: Establish a plan of action and implement solution. Step 5: Verify full functionality and implement preventive measures. Step 6: Document findings, actions, and outcomes.

1. Identify the problem (gather info, question user, identify symptoms, duplicate if possible, check environmental/infrastructure changes). 2. Establish a theory of probable cause. 3. Test the theory (if confirmed, proceed; if not, establish new theory or escalate). 4. Establish a plan of action, implement the solution. 5. Verify full system functionality, implement preventative measures. 6. Document findings, actions, and outcomes.

Batch IF: IF "%1"=="yes" echo Confirmed. PowerShell: if ($variable -eq "yes") { ... }. Python: if variable == "yes":. Bash: if [ "$variable" = "yes" ]; then. Enable scripts to take different actions based on conditions (file exists, variable value, command success/failure).

Do not discuss customer or company information outside of work context. If you overhear confidential business conversations while on-site, maintain discretion — do not repeat or act on overheard information. Applies to personal information about customers as well.
MDM-delivered policy packages. Enforce: screen lock, encryption, VPN, Wi-Fi, email, certificate distribution, app restrictions. Users CANNOT modify profile-enforced settings.

Wi-Fi: toggle airplane mode off/on, forget and re-join network, check IP config (DHCP vs static). Bluetooth: unpair and re-pair device, clear Bluetooth cache (Android: Settings > Apps > Bluetooth > Storage > Clear Cache). Cellular: check SIM card is fully seated, check APN settings (carrier settings for mobile data), check roaming settings for international travel.

Wi-Fi: toggle airplane mode on/off to reset radios, forget and rejoin network, check IP configuration (DHCP vs static). Bluetooth: unpair and re-pair device, clear Bluetooth cache (Android). Cellular: check roaming settings, APN configuration (for mobile data), SIM card seated properly. GPS: enable location services, check app permissions for location access. NFC: enable in settings, hold device flat against NFC target.

Lightweight application virtualization. Share host OS kernel — no separate OS per container. Much faster startup and less overhead than VMs. Image: template defining the container environment. Container: running instance of an image. Docker Compose: multi-container app definition. Kubernetes: orchestration platform for running and managing containers at scale. Use case: microservices, DevOps, consistent development-to-production environments.

PC boots, crashes, restarts repeatedly. Causes: Windows update failure (automatic repair should kick in after 2 failures), bad RAM, corrupted system files, overheating causing thermal shutdown immediately. Use WinRE to run Startup Repair. If RAM: run memtest86+. Check CPU temperatures with case open if thermal issue suspected.

Legacy interface still required for: Internet Options, Indexing Options, Network and Sharing Center, Power Options, Programs and Features, Mail applet, Administrative Tools. Some items have no equivalent in Settings.

CPU cooler must match socket (mounting pattern) and TDP. Aftermarket cooler: replaces stock/boxed cooler for better performance or quieter operation. Stock coolers included with most retail CPUs — adequate for normal operation. High-end CPUs (125W+) benefit significantly from aftermarket air or AIO liquid coolers.

Core: physical processing unit. Multi-core CPU contains multiple independent cores on one die. Thread: logical processor. Hyperthreading (Intel) / SMT — Simultaneous Multi-Threading (AMD): each physical core handles 2 threads simultaneously. A 6-core/12-thread CPU appears as 12 logical CPUs to the OS. More cores = better multi-threaded workload performance. Higher clock speed = better single-threaded workload performance.

Laptop CPUs: most modern laptops have CPUs soldered to motherboard (BGA — Ball Grid Array packaging). Not user-replaceable. Cooling: heat pipe transfers heat from CPU die to fins, fan exhausts from vent. Thermal paste between CPU die and heat pipe contact plate. Over time, thermal paste dries and needs replacement — symptom: high temps, thermal throttling, unexpected shutdown under load.

Central Processing Unit — executes program instructions. Modern CPUs contain: multiple cores (physical processing units), L1/L2/L3 cache (see 3.2), integrated memory controller, integrated graphics (on some CPUs), PCIe controller. Main vendors: Intel (Core i-series, Xeon for server) and AMD (Ryzen for consumer, EPYC for server).

Socket is CPU-generation-specific. Intel: LGA1700 (12th/13th/14th gen Alder/Raptor/Meteor Lake). LGA1200 (10th/11th gen). AMD: AM4 (Ryzen 1000–5000 series). AM5 (Ryzen 7000 series, LGA). Server: Intel LGA4189 (Xeon Scalable), AMD SP3 (EPYC). Check compatibility before purchasing — CPU, motherboard, and RAM must all be compatible.

Intel LGA (Land Grid Array): pins are in the socket, CPU has flat pads. LGA1700 (12th/13th/14th gen Intel). Fragile socket pins — do not drop CPU into socket. AMD PGA (Pin Grid Array): pins on the CPU bottom (AM4 socket). Going away: AM5 uses LGA like Intel. Socket is CPU-generation specific — check compatibility before purchase.

CPU rarely fails on its own. More common: bent pins on AMD AM4 socket (inspect carefully — use magnifier), incompatible CPU/motherboard combination, CPU improperly seated. No-name third-party CPU cooler causing intermittent contact = poor thermal transfer. If CPU fan not detected: motherboard may refuse to boot (BIOS protection). Check CPU fan header connection.

VT-x (Intel Virtualization Technology) or AMD-V (AMD Virtualization) hardware extensions. All modern CPUs support this but it may be disabled in BIOS. Must enable in BIOS/UEFI before hypervisor can run (especially Type 2 — Type 1 may bypass this check). VT-d (Intel) / AMD-Vi: IOMMU for PCIe passthrough — allows physical GPU or NIC to be dedicated to a specific VM.

CRT (Cathode Ray Tube) monitors contain capacitors that can store lethal voltages (25,000–30,000 volts) even when unplugged for months or years. Never open a CRT without proper training and discharge equipment. Discharge the CRT capacitor using a high-voltage discharge tool before working inside. CompTIA exam context: technicians should be aware of this risk and not casually open CRTs.
Hijacks CPU/GPU to mine cryptocurrency. Symptoms: high CPU/GPU utilization, heat, fan noise, degraded performance, increased power consumption — with no user activity.

Uses victim's CPU/GPU to mine cryptocurrency for attacker. Symptoms: CPU pegged at 95–100% even when idle, elevated GPU usage, computer runs hot, fans at full speed, very slow performance, higher electricity usage. Investigate with Task Manager (Details tab for specific process). Often disguised as legitimate process name or hidden in browser via malicious JavaScript.

Organizations classify data by sensitivity: Public (freely shareable) → Internal → Confidential → Restricted/Secret. Classification determines handling requirements, access controls, and disposal methods. Technicians should not access data above their clearance level.

After drive failure: professional data recovery services (Ontrack, DriveSavers) for mechanically failed drives — expensive ($300–$1500+). Software recovery: Recuva, R-Studio for logical failures (file system corruption, accidental deletion) — much cheaper, success depends on whether sectors overwritten. Backup is the only reliable prevention — recovery services cannot always recover data.
BitLocker (Windows), FileVault (macOS), LUKS (Linux). Encrypts drive — physical theft doesn't expose data. Required for portable devices with sensitive data.

DDR3: 240-pin DIMM, 1.5V (DDR3L = 1.35V low voltage), speeds 800–2133 MT/s, older systems. DDR4: 288-pin DIMM, 1.2V, speeds 2133–3200+ MT/s (XMP profiles push higher), current mainstream. Notch position different from DDR3 — physically cannot install in wrong slot. DDR5: 288-pin DIMM (different notch from DDR4), 1.1V, 4800+ MT/s, on-die ECC, power management on DIMM. Not backward compatible with DDR4 slots. Each generation requires matching motherboard and CPU support.

Dead pixel: always black (transistor failed — pixel permanently off). Stuck pixel: permanently lit in one color (red, green, or blue — pixel element stuck on). Stuck pixels may be fixable with pixel-unstick software (flashes rapidly-changing colors). Dead pixels are permanent hardware defects. Monitor warranty coverage varies — some manufacturers cover single dead pixel, others require a minimum count.
Be aware that communication styles, personal space norms, and eye contact expectations vary across cultures. Remain respectful, patient, and non-judgmental. Avoid assumptions.

IP address of the router interface on the local subnet. All traffic destined for outside the local subnet is sent to the default gateway for routing. If default gateway is wrong or unreachable: can reach local devices but not internet or other subnets.

Powerful electromagnetic field randomizes magnetic domains. Effective on HDDs and magnetic tape ONLY. DOES NOT WORK ON SSDs — flash has no magnetic properties. Also destroys HDD servo tracks — drive cannot be reused after degaussing.
iOS: enabled by default when passcode is set. Android: typically default on modern devices. Encrypts internal storage — protects against physical theft and forensic extraction.

Shows all hardware organized by category. Status icons: yellow triangle with ! = driver problem or device conflict. Red X = device disabled. No overlay = functioning normally. Actions: Update Driver, Roll Back Driver (reverts to previous version), Disable, Enable, Uninstall (then scan for hardware changes to reinstall). Troubleshooting sequence: update driver → roll back driver → uninstall and reinstall → check Windows Update.

MDM (Mobile Device Management) enforces enterprise security policies: require PIN/password (minimum complexity and length), enforce encryption, block camera, block screen capture, prevent app sideloading, remotely wipe device if lost/stolen, detect rooted/jailbroken devices and block enrollment, enforce VPN usage, push certificates.

Automatically assigns IP configuration to network clients. Lease: time-limited IP assignment — client must renew before expiry. DORA: Discover (UDP broadcast, client has no IP yet) → Offer (server proposes IP from scope) → Request (client accepts offer, broadcasts to let other DHCP servers know) → Acknowledge (server confirms, updates lease table). Scope: defined range of IPs available. Exclusions: IPs within scope withheld from DHCP pool (for static devices). Reservations: MAC address to IP binding — specific device always gets same IP via DHCP. Option 3: default gateway. Option 6: DNS server. Option 15: domain name.
Tries common words and known password patterns from breach databases. More efficient than pure brute force. Mitigated by complex passwords and breach-list checking.

Copies all data that has changed since the LAST FULL BACKUP (regardless of intervening differentials). Archive bit NOT cleared — each differential grows larger than the last. Restore requires: last full + last differential (2 backup sets). Faster to back up than full. Slower to restore than incremental (but faster than full incremental chain).

Display (LCD/OLED panel): the visual component — produces the image. Digitizer: the transparent touch-sensing layer that detects finger/stylus input. These are separate components (though often sold bonded together for repair). Symptom: screen looks fine but touch input is wrong/unresponsive = digitizer failed. Symptom: display is cracked/discolored but touch still works = display failed. Symptom: touch registers in wrong location = digitizer misalignment or damage (requires replacement).

Check brightness setting (Fn key combination or Windows brightness slider). Power plan may reduce brightness on battery. Failing backlight: display visible with flashlight held close at an angle in dark room. If backlight failed: repair or replace display panel/backlight assembly.
Automatically executes programs when removable media inserted. Responsible for widespread malware. Disabled by default in Windows 7+ — verify via Group Policy in enterprise.
Passwordless access — disabled by default in Windows 10/11 but verify. Enabled guest account = unauthorized local access foothold.
Every service = potential attack vector. Disable RDP if not needed, Telnet on all systems (plaintext), Print Spooler on non-printing servers. Document what is disabled and why.

Universal Plug and Play allows devices to automatically open router ports without user approval. Malware can exploit this. Disable UPnP. Configure port forwarding manually only for specific required services.

Graphical storage configuration. Tasks: initialize new drives (MBR or GPT), create/delete partitions, format volumes (NTFS/FAT32/exFAT), assign/change drive letters, extend or shrink volumes, convert basic to dynamic disk, set active partition, view health status. Cannot recover deleted partitions — requires third-party tools.

Located: /Applications/Utilities. Format and partition drives, run First Aid (verify/repair disk errors), create and restore disk images (.dmg). macOS equivalent of Windows Disk Management plus disk repair.

Repairs the Windows component store (WinSxS) that SFC draws from. Key commands: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth — detects corruption. DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /ScanHealth — full scan. DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth — repairs using Windows Update as source. Use DISM first if SFC fails repeatedly. Requires internet access (uses Windows Update) or mounted Windows ISO as source.

eDP (embedded DisplayPort): standard internal display connection in modern laptops. Display assembly: panel + bezel + hinges + antenna wires. Replacing just the panel: unscrew bezel clips, lift panel, disconnect eDP cable (ZIF or push connector), disconnect antenna wires from wireless card. CCFL backlight (legacy) vs LED backlight (modern) — not interchangeable.

HD: 1280×720 (720p). FHD: 1920×1080 (1080p) — standard for most laptops. QHD: 2560×1440 (1440p). 4K UHD: 3840×2160. Higher resolution on smaller screen = higher PPI = sharper image but increased GPU/battery load.

Resolution: must match native panel resolution for sharpest image. Scaling: Windows Display Settings scale for HiDPI (125%, 150%, 200%). Color calibration: OS or hardware colorimeter calibration. Brightness and contrast: adjust for ambient light. Refresh rate: set in Display Settings > Advanced Display > Refresh Rate. Multiple displays: extended (separate desktops), duplicate (mirror), or single display modes.

Debian-based: Ubuntu, Debian, Linux Mint. Package manager: apt/apt-get. Package format: .deb. Debian is known for stability; Ubuntu for user-friendliness. Red Hat-based: RHEL (Red Hat Enterprise Linux), Fedora, CentOS. Package manager: yum (older) or dnf (modern). Package format: .rpm. RHEL is enterprise-grade; Fedora is cutting-edge. SUSE-based: openSUSE, SLES. Package manager: zypper. Arch-based: Arch Linux. Package manager: pacman.

Physical media (DVD/Blu-ray): legacy, fixed version, update after install. ISO files: disk image — mount natively in Windows 10/11 by right-clicking → Mount. Appears as a virtual optical drive. Downloadable packages: .exe (self-contained Windows executable), .msi (Windows Installer package — supports silent install with msiexec). macOS: .dmg (drag to Applications), .pkg (installer wizard). Linux: .deb (Debian/Ubuntu), .rpm (Red Hat/Fedora) — package managers handle dependencies automatically. App stores: Microsoft Store, Mac App Store — curated, automatic updates. Image deployment: enterprise — preconfigured OS image with all apps baked in.

Isolate problem to a specific layer or component. Binary approach: test midpoint of a system to halve the problem space. Network: ping loopback → gateway → external IP → hostname (each test isolates a specific layer). Hardware: swap components one at a time (change one variable at a time to isolate cause).

Public-facing servers placed between internet and internal network. Compromise of DMZ server does not reach internal network. Separate zone with router enforcing rules between external, DMZ, and internal.

Translates human-readable hostnames to IP addresses. Hierarchical distributed database. Resolution process: client queries local DNS cache → local DNS resolver (ISP or internal) → recursive query through root → TLD → authoritative server. TTL (Time To Live): how long a DNS record is cached. DNS record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail server, with priority value), CNAME (canonical alias — multiple names to one A record), PTR (reverse lookup, IP to hostname), NS (authoritative name server for zone), TXT (text records — SPF, DKIM, DMARC for email authentication, domain verification).

Primary DNS: first DNS server queried. Secondary/Alternate DNS: queried if primary fails. Common public DNS: Google (8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4), Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), ISP-provided. Enterprise: internal DNS server for private zones + forwards to external DNS for public resolution.

Symptom: can ping IP addresses (8.8.8.8) but not hostnames (google.com) — DNS failure. Fix: ipconfig /flushdns (clears stale cache). Check DNS server setting in ipconfig /all — must point to valid DNS server. Test with nslookup [hostname] [alternate DNS] to bypass local resolver. Change DNS to 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1 to test if internal DNS server is the problem.
Corrupt DNS cache with false IPs — legitimate domain queries return attacker-controlled IPs. Redirects without visible URL change.

Translates domain names to IP addresses. Without DNS: can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot load google.com. Exam scenario: user can access sites by IP but not by name = DNS problem. Check with nslookup and ipconfig /displaydns.

Connect via Thunderbolt/USB-C single cable. Provide: multiple USB-A ports, Ethernet, display outputs (HDMI, DP), audio, card reader, power delivery to laptop. Proprietary docking: Surface Connect (Microsoft), barrel connector on older Dell/HP/Lenovo — single-vendor. Universal USB-C/TB docking: cross-platform compatibility.

Every change — successful or failed — must be documented: what was changed, when, by whom, what the result was, what issues arose. Failed changes with successful rollback are still documented. Documentation feeds future impact analyses and post-incident reviews.

Client-server enterprise networking. Active Directory Domain Controller (DC) manages all user accounts centrally. Users authenticate once to the DC and receive access to all authorized resources — Single Sign-On (SSO). Group Policy pushes configuration from DC to all domain-joined machines. Domain join requires Windows Pro or higher — Home CANNOT join a domain. Scalable to thousands of machines.

DoS: single-source flood exhausting target resources. DDoS: botnet-scale flood from thousands of distributed sources — source-based blocking ineffective. DDoS requires upstream ISP-level or cloud scrubbing mitigation.
Browser downloads from official vendor sites only. Verify hash (MD5/SHA-256) against vendor-published hash. Third-party aggregators may bundle adware/PUPs/modified installers.

Main system memory type. "Dynamic" because it requires constant refresh cycles to retain data (unlike SRAM which is static but more expensive). Each bit stored as charge in a capacitor that leaks — must be refreshed thousands of times per second. All DDR variants are DRAM.
Drill press through HDD platters destroys magnetic surface. Effective for individual drives. Can be applied to SSDs but less thorough than shredding.

Check: SATA data cable firmly connected at both ends. SATA power cable connected. Try different SATA port on motherboard. Check BIOS storage mode (AHCI vs IDE — AHCI recommended for modern SSDs). For M.2: verify screw is securing the drive, check PCIe/SATA compatibility with slot. New drive: may appear but show unallocated — initialize in Disk Management before use.

Older PSUs have a physical 115V/230V selector switch. Setting wrong: 115V PSU on 230V circuit = immediate PSU damage. 230V PSU on 115V = PSU may not turn on or output at half voltage. Modern switching PSUs auto-detect input voltage (90V–264V range) — no switch needed.

Recovering sensitive material from discarded waste. Network diagrams, invoices, employee directories, sticky-note passwords, improperly discarded drives. Mitigation: cross-cut shredding, certified media destruction.

Two devices configured with same IP. Windows: balloon notification "IP address conflict" and event log error. Symptoms: intermittent connectivity (both devices lose network as ARP conflict occurs). Resolution: identify static IP devices on network, change one to different IP. Check for static IP that overlaps DHCP scope — add exclusion in DHCP for that IP.

Electronic waste (e-waste) includes: CRT and LCD monitors, computers, printers, batteries (Li-ion, NiMH, lead-acid), toner cartridges, smartphones. E-waste contains hazardous materials: lead (CRT glass), mercury (fluorescent backlights), cadmium, beryllium. Cannot be placed in regular trash. Disposal options: manufacturer take-back programs, certified e-waste recyclers, municipal e-waste collection events, retail drop-off programs (Best Buy). Regulations vary by state/locality.

Detects and corrects single-bit memory errors. Adds extra data bits per byte for parity checking. Used in servers and workstations where data integrity is critical. Requires ECC-capable CPU and motherboard (Intel Xeon, AMD EPYC, Ryzen Pro). Consumer platforms typically do not support ECC. Registered (RDIMM): additional buffer chip on DIMM — reduces electrical load on CPU memory controller, supports higher capacities. Used in servers.

Feature / Home / Pro / Enterprise: BitLocker: No/Yes/Yes. Group Policy (gpedit.msc): No/Yes/Yes. Domain Join: No/Yes/Yes. RDP Server (host): No/Yes/Yes. App-V: No/No/Yes. DirectAccess: No/No/Yes. Credential Guard: No/No/Yes. Max RAM (64-bit): 128 GB / 2 TB / 6 TB.

Internal display interface standard. Connects display panel to GPU via flat ribbon cable inside the laptop chassis. Supports DisplayPort features (high refresh rates, HDR, high resolutions) over an internal interface. Replaced LVDS (Low-Voltage Differential Signaling) in modern laptops.

Endpoint Detection and Response. Behavioral monitoring on endpoints. Detects anomalous process behavior, network connections, API calls. Detects fileless and zero-day threats. Provides response capabilities (isolate, terminate, rollback).
File-level encryption on NTFS. Transparent to authorized user. Tied to user certificate. PERMANENTLY INACCESSIBLE if certificate lost — without Data Recovery Agent. Pro and above only.

File-level encryption on NTFS volumes. Encrypts individual files/folders — NOT the whole drive. Transparent to the authorized user (opens/saves normally). Encryption tied to user account's encryption certificate stored in user profile. CRITICAL: if the account is deleted, certificate is lost/corrupted, or profile corrupts = files are PERMANENTLY INACCESSIBLE without a recovery agent. Available Windows Pro and above. Use a DRA (Data Recovery Agent) in enterprise to enable administrative recovery.

No food or drinks near electronic equipment. Do not work on live circuits unless specifically trained. Ground all equipment before servicing. Use GFCI (Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter) outlets in damp locations. Label circuits before working on them. Power off and unplug before opening equipment (except for hot-swap components).
Enterprise Mobility Management. Umbrella term: MDM + MAM + identity management.
Server rack locks secure physical enclosures housing servers and networking equipment. Prevents physical access to systems, USB ports, and console connections.

External SATA. Shielded, longer-reach version of SATA for external drives. Port looks similar to internal SATA but different connector keying. Provides native SATA speed to external drive. Does NOT provide power (separate power connector or eSATAp combo port). Largely replaced by USB 3.0 and Thunderbolt for external storage.

When issue is beyond your skill, authority, or access: escalate to appropriate tier or specialist. Document what you have already tried before escalating — prevents repeat work. Know your escalation path in your organization.

Static electricity discharge that can permanently damage or destroy sensitive electronic components (CPU, RAM, expansion cards, drives). Invisible and painless to humans but destructive to components. Prevention: antistatic wrist strap (connects technician to chassis ground), antistatic mat (grounded work surface), antistatic bags (for transport and storage), touch the chassis before handling components to equalize charge.

ls: list directory contents (ls -la = all files including hidden, long format). pwd: print working directory. cd: change directory (cd .. = up one, cd / = root, cd ~ = home). cp: copy (cp -r for directories). mv: move or rename. rm: remove (rm -r = recursive directories, rm -f = force). mkdir: make directory. chmod: change permissions. chown: change ownership. grep: search text patterns in files. find: find files. cat: display file contents. man: manual pages. sudo: run as superuser. ps: list processes. top: interactive process monitor.

Legal agreement between software vendor and user defining permitted use, restrictions, and limitations. Typically: single machine use (unless volume license), no redistribution, no reverse engineering, limited to named user or device. Violation = breach of license = potential legal liability.

Windows logging system. Four main Windows Logs: Application (program events), Security (logon/logoff, policy changes, privilege use), System (driver failures, service issues, hardware events), Setup (installation events). Event levels: Information (success), Warning (potential future problem), Error (significant problem), Critical (severe failure). Every event has an Event ID — searchable for specific cause and resolution. Key IDs: 41 = unexpected/dirty shutdown, 4720 = user account created, 4624 = successful logon, 4625 = failed logon, 1001 = Windows Error Reporting.

Windows Logs > System: OS events, driver failures, service crashes — best source for BSOD and hardware error info. Windows Logs > Application: app-specific errors and crashes. Windows Logs > Security: logon/logoff, policy changes, account events. Custom Views > Administrative Events: critical + error + warning events from all logs in one view. After BSOD, check System log for Critical event around the crash time.
Rogue AP with same SSID as legitimate network. Devices auto-connect based on SSID matching. Traffic intercepted by attacker. Mitigation: VPN on untrusted networks, manual connection approval.

Must memorize the 8-step sequence in order. Exam will present steps out of order and ask you to sequence them. Key sequences: Quarantine (2) comes BEFORE remediation (4). Disable System Restore (3) comes BEFORE scanning (4). Enable System Restore (6) comes AFTER remediation (4) and updates (5). Educate (7) and Document (8) always last.

"BOOTMGR is missing" or "Operating system not found" = bootrec /fixmbr and bootrec /rebuildbcd from WinRE. System files corrupted = SFC /scannow. SFC keeps failing = DISM /RestoreHealth first, then SFC. Cannot boot at all = WinRE Startup Repair first. Last resort = Reset This PC or clean install.
Any scenario mentioning more than 4 GB RAM = must be 64-bit OS. Any scenario involving App-V, DirectAccess, or Credential Guard = Enterprise edition answer.

Changed homepage/redirects = browser hijacker. Fake AV demanding payment = scareware/rogue antivirus. .locked files + ransom note = ransomware. 100% CPU when idle = cryptominer. Popups with no browser = adware. Hosts file modified = DNS hijack via hosts. Proxy changed = traffic interception malware. Windows Defender disabled = advanced malware/rootkit. New unknown accounts = backdoor/compromise.
For app problems, exam follows: Force Stop → Clear Cache → Clear Data → Reinstall → Update OS → Factory Reset. Never jump to factory reset without exhausting simpler options first.

DDR3 = 240-pin DIMM. DDR4 = 288-pin DIMM. DDR5 = 288-pin DIMM (different notch). SODIMM DDR4 = 260-pin. Each generation has different notch position — cannot install wrong generation in a slot (keying prevents it). Match RAM to motherboard specification.
Rooting = Android. Jailbreaking = iOS. Both achieve same goal: privileged OS access. Both remove security restrictions. Both can be detected by MDM and enterprise apps.

Extended FAT — modern replacement for FAT32 on removable media. Cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux with driver). No 4 GB file size limit. No practical volume size limit. No journaling or security features. Best choice for USB drives and SD cards shared between Windows and macOS. Exam answer for "cross-platform removable media without 4 GB limit."

Fourth Extended Filesystem — Linux default. Journaling, max volume 1 exabyte, max file 16 TB. Not natively supported on Windows or macOS without third-party drivers. Most common Linux filesystem on the exam.

HDMI: digital audio + video, most universal. Mini HDMI or full HDMI on laptops. Versions: 1.4 (4K@30Hz), 2.0 (4K@60Hz), 2.1 (4K@120Hz/8K support). DisplayPort / Mini DisplayPort: higher bandwidth than HDMI, supports daisy-chaining (MST), no royalty fee. USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode): video output via USB-C port using DP protocol. Thunderbolt 3/4 (USB-C): supports video output + high-speed data + power delivery on a single cable. VGA: analog, legacy, no audio — requires active adapter for digital conversion.

Laser: toner low — gently shake toner cartridge side to side to redistribute remaining toner (temporary fix — replace cartridge). Density setting too low in driver settings. Inkjet: ink low, or head partially clogged.
iOS: configurable erase after 10 failed attempts. Android: increasing delays. Enforced via MDM.

CPUFAN: primary CPU cooler fan header — mandatory connection. System monitors CPU fan speed; no fan connected = potential overcooling alarm or boot failure. SYSFAN / CHA_FAN: case fan headers. PWM (Pulse Width Modulation): 4-pin header — motherboard controls fan speed via PWM signal. DC control: 3-pin header — speed controlled by voltage. 4-pin fan works in 3-pin header (no speed control).

File Allocation Table 32 — legacy, cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux all read/write). Critical limitations: max individual file size = 4 GB (a single file over 4 GB cannot be stored on FAT32). Max volume size: 2 TB (Windows formats up to 32 GB; use diskpart for larger). No permissions, no journaling, no encryption. Use for: legacy USB devices, older hardware compatibility.

LC (Local Connector / Lucent Connector): small form factor, snap-in latch, most common in modern data center equipment. SC (Subscriber Connector): push-pull, square body, older but still common. ST (Straight Tip): push-and-twist bayonet mount, older, used in legacy installations. MT-RJ: duplex connector (both fibers in one connector body). FC: screw-on, used in test equipment and single-mode telecom.

Transmits data as light pulses through glass/plastic core. Immune to EMI, no ground loops, supports longer distances than copper. Two types: Single-mode (SMF): 9 micron core, laser light source, yellow outer jacket (standard), supports distances up to 100 km. For WAN, campus backbone, data center interconnects. Multimode (MMF): 50 or 62.5 micron core, LED light source, orange or aqua jacket, up to 2 km. For shorter runs (building to building, patch within data center). SMF is more expensive than MMF.

Two exam-critical settings: (1) "Hide extensions for known file types" — DISABLE this. Malware hides as document.pdf.exe appearing as just "document" with PDF icon when extensions are hidden. (2) "Show hidden files, folders, and drives" — ENABLE for troubleshooting to access AppData, ProgramData, OS config files. Keep "Hide protected OS files" enabled during normal use.

Hosts shared files accessible over network. Windows: SMB (port 445) via UNC path (\\server\share). Linux: Samba (SMB compatibility), NFS (Network File System). Permissions: NTFS permissions (granular, applied on disk) vs share permissions (applied at share level) — more restrictive of the two applies.
Lives entirely in RAM — no executable file on disk. Uses legitimate system tools: PowerShell, WMI, LOLbins. Traditional file-based AV cannot detect it. Requires EDR behavioral monitoring.

Internal Windows drive → NTFS. USB/SD card for cross-platform use → exFAT. USB with legacy device compatibility → FAT32 (accept 4 GB limit). Linux internal drive → ext4. macOS/iOS → APFS. Microsoft enterprise resilient storage → ReFS.

Full-disk encryption using XTS-AES-128 with 256-bit key. Encrypts the entire startup disk. Generates a recovery key — must be stored securely. Enable: System Settings > Privacy and Security. macOS equivalent of BitLocker.
macOS file manager — equivalent to Windows File Explorer. Navigates files, folders, applications, network shares, and connected devices.

Class A: ordinary combustibles (wood, paper, cloth, plastic) — water, foam. Class B: flammable liquids (gasoline, paint, grease) — CO2, dry chemical. Class C: electrical equipment fires — CO2, dry chemical (non-conductive). "C = Current (electrical)." Class D: combustible metals (magnesium, titanium) — dry powder only. Class K: cooking oils and fats (commercial kitchens) — wet chemical. Multipurpose ABC extinguisher covers most common scenarios. CO2 best for electronics (leaves no residue).

Filters traffic based on rules (ACLs — Access Control Lists). Stateless: filters each packet independently based on IP/port rules. Stateful: tracks connection state — allows return traffic for established sessions. Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW): Layer 7 inspection, application awareness, IDS/IPS integration, user-based policies. Default-deny: block all traffic except explicitly permitted. Default-allow: permit all except explicitly blocked. Default-deny is more secure.

Symptom: specific application cannot connect while others work fine. Test: temporarily disable firewall and test application — if works = firewall rule needed. Re-enable firewall, add appropriate rule (application exception or specific port). Check both Windows Firewall (on client) and network firewall (on router/appliance). Ports blocked: verify application's required ports in documentation.
Default-deny policy. Disable unused ports. Minimize port forwarding rules (each creates an external-to-internal path). Enable SPI (Stateful Packet Inspection).
Inbound: controls what reaches the system. Outbound: controls what the system sends. Rules by port, protocol, application, profile. wf.msc = Windows Firewall with Advanced Security.
Router firmware has security patches. Check manufacturer site. Enable auto-update if supported. Unpatched router firmware = primary attack target.

USB flash drive: USB Type-A or Type-C. USB 3.0 minimum for reasonable speed. SD cards: standard sizes — SD (full size), miniSD (rare), microSD (phones/cameras). Speed classes: Class 10 (10 MB/s), UHS-I (104 MB/s), UHS-II (312 MB/s), V30 (30 MB/s write minimum — minimum for 4K video recording).

Causes: loose video cable connection, refresh rate mismatch (set correct Hz in Display Settings), failing backlight (laptop), interference (analog VGA near electrical noise source). Fix: reseat cable, set correct refresh rate, test different cable.

After resolving an issue: follow up with the user (call or email) to confirm the issue is fully resolved and they are satisfied. Do not close a ticket without confirming resolution with the user. Follow-through builds trust and catches cases where the original fix did not fully resolve the issue.
Opens Force Quit Applications window for terminating frozen apps. Equivalent to End Task in Windows Task Manager.

Small pin headers on motherboard for case connections: PWRSW (power button), RESET (reset button), PWRLED (power LED), HDDLED (drive activity LED), SPEAKER (PC speaker for beep codes), USB 2.0 headers (internal USB), USB 3.0 header (internal USB), HDAUDIO (front panel headphone/mic). Must be connected correctly — consult motherboard manual for pin layout.

Soft reset (force restart): does NOT erase data. Method varies: iPhone 8+: volume up, volume down, hold side button. Android: hold power + volume down for 10 seconds (varies by manufacturer). Separate from factory reset (erases all data). Try soft reset before any other troubleshooting step for frozen device.

Copies all selected data regardless of change status. Archive bit cleared after backup. Restore requires: 1 tape/backup set. Fastest to restore. Slowest to back up. Most storage-intensive. Typically done weekly or monthly as the baseline for other backup types.

term: Full vs Differential vs Incremental comparison
