Data split across 2+ disks in chunks. Read/write performance: best (parallel access to all disks). Redundancy: NONE. One drive fails = entire array fails, all data lost. Capacity: sum of all drives. Use when: maximum performance needed, data loss acceptable (scratch disks, temp storage).

Exact copy of data on 2 drives simultaneously. Redundancy: 1 drive failure tolerated. Read performance: can be improved (read from either drive). Write performance: same as single drive (must write to both). Usable capacity: 50% of total (2 × 2TB drives = 2TB usable). Use when: data integrity critical, small array.

Nested RAID: RAID 1 (mirrored pairs) combined with RAID 0 (striping across pairs). Minimum 4 drives (2 pairs). Redundancy: 1 drive per mirrored pair can fail. Read/write performance: excellent. Usable capacity: 50%. Most expensive but best performance + redundancy. Used in high-performance, high-availability databases.

Data and parity information striped across 3+ drives. Minimum 3 drives. Parity allows reconstruction of failed drive. Redundancy: 1 drive failure tolerated. Usable capacity: (N-1) × drive size. Example: 4 × 2TB = 6TB usable. Good balance of performance, redundancy, and capacity efficiency. Rebuild time: hours to days depending on array size — vulnerable during rebuild.

Like RAID 5 but with two parity calculations. Minimum 4 drives. Redundancy: 2 simultaneous drive failures tolerated. Usable capacity: (N-2) × drive size. Better for large arrays where rebuild time = higher risk of second failure. Write performance slower than RAID 5 (double parity calculation).

One drive in RAID has failed — array still operates (RAID 1, 5, 6, 10) but without redundancy. Indicator: RAID management utility shows degraded/degraded status, warning light on hot-swap drive bay, event log alert. Action: identify and replace failed drive promptly. RAID 5/6 rebuild: controller reconstructs data on new drive using parity — takes hours to days. During rebuild: performance impact + increased risk of second drive failure (read stress on remaining drives).

RAID protects against drive hardware failure ONLY. RAID does not protect against: accidental deletion, file corruption, ransomware (encrypts all files including RAID array), fire/flood (same physical location). Backup is required in addition to RAID.
Precomputed hash database to reverse password hashes. Defeated by SALTING (adding random value before hashing).

Laptops use SODIMM (Small Outline DIMM) — physically smaller than desktop DIMM. DDR4 SODIMM: 260 pins. DDR5 SODIMM: 262 pins. Installed at an angle (~30–45°) and pressed down to lock into retention clips. Many modern thin laptops have RAM soldered directly to motherboard — non-upgradeable. Check before purchasing if RAM upgrade is planned.

DDR generation-specific (DDR4 slots ≠ DDR5 slots). Typically 2 or 4 slots on consumer boards. Slot color coding for dual-channel: install 2 sticks in matching colors (often A2 + B2 slots). Check motherboard manual for recommended slot population order.

Verify RAM seated fully in correct slots (dual-channel slots). Test one stick at a time to identify faulty stick. memtest86+: bootable USB tool — tests entire RAM with comprehensive error patterns. Run for at minimum 2 full passes. Any errors = defective RAM. Symptoms of bad RAM: random BSOD (especially PAGEFAULT or MEMORYMANAGEMENT stop codes), application crashes, file corruption, system instability.

Encrypts victim files with strong cryptography. Demands cryptocurrency payment for decryption key. Defense: 3-2-1 backup rule. Response: DO NOT PAY. Disconnect immediately. Restore from clean offline backup. Symptom: changed file extensions (.locked/.encrypted), ransom note file.

Files renamed with unfamiliar extension (.locked, .encrypted, .crypt, .[[attacker-email]]) — original content inaccessible. Ransom note file (README.txt, HOWTODECRYPT.html) in folders or on desktop. May display fullscreen lockscreen with payment demand. Immediate action: disconnect from network to prevent spread. Do NOT pay — no guarantee of key. Restore from backup.

Microsoft proprietary protocol for graphical remote desktop sessions. Default port: 3389 (TCP). Encrypted by default (TLS/NLA). Requires: Remote Desktop enabled on target machine, firewall rule allowing port 3389, user must be in Remote Desktop Users group (or be admin). Windows Home cannot HOST RDP sessions — can only connect as client. Pro and Enterprise can host.

Reset This PC — Keep My Files: reinstalls Windows, preserves personal files, removes apps. Reset This PC — Remove Everything: reinstalls Windows, deletes all user data. OEM recovery partition: restores factory image including original OS and OEM software — partition is lost if drive is replaced.
Hz — display update frequency per second. 60 Hz standard. 120/144/165/240 Hz on gaming laptops. Higher refresh = smoother motion. Requires GPU support at that resolution + refresh rate.

Refresh rate (Hz): how many times per second the display updates. 60 Hz = standard. 120/144/165/240 Hz = gaming. Higher Hz = smoother motion, lower input lag. Requires matching GPU output at that resolution and refresh rate. Response time (ms): time for pixel to transition between colors. Lower = less motion blur/ghosting. GtG (gray-to-gray) is the most common measurement.

Resilient File System — Microsoft enterprise filesystem. Automatically detects and repairs data corruption. Available as local drive on Windows Pro for Workstations and Server. Does NOT support: compression, disk quotas, file-level encryption (EFS). Designed for data integrity over long-term storage workloads.

Windows Registry = hierarchical configuration database. Five hives (root keys): HKEYCLASSESROOT (HKCR) — file associations and COM objects. HKEYCURRENTUSER (HKCU) — per-user settings for the logged-in user. HKEYLOCALMACHINE (HKLM) — system-wide hardware and software configuration (most important for administration). HKEYUSERS (HKU) — profile data for all accounts. HKEYCURRENTCONFIG (HKCC) — current hardware profile. Structure: Keys (folders) → Subkeys (nested folders) → Values (individual settings). Value types: REGSZ (string/text), REGDWORD (32-bit number), REGBINARY (raw binary). CRITICAL: Always export the key before modifying. Wrong deletion can make Windows unbootable.

Industries with specific documentation requirements: HIPAA (healthcare — audit logs of PHI access), PCI-DSS (payment — network diagrams, access control records), SOX (finance — change control records). Documentation must be retained per regulatory schedule and may be subpoenaed.

HIPAA: PHI must be unreadable/unrecoverable before hardware disposal. PCI-DSS: specific destruction requirements for cardholder data. EPA: e-waste regulations — hazardous materials (lead, mercury, cadmium) must not enter landfills. Use EPEAT or R2/e-Stewards certified recyclers.

When malware cannot be fully removed (advanced rootkit, UEFI/firmware-level malware, deep system compromise) — wipe and reinstall the OS from a clean image. Restore user data from a clean backup made before infection. Most reliable method to guarantee full removal.
iCloud (iOS), Google Drive (Android). Automatic device backup. Enables restore to replacement after wipe. Verify backups are current.

Port 3389 TCP. Enable in System Properties > Remote tab > Allow remote connections. Requires user to be in Remote Desktop Users group (or be an Administrator). NLA (Network Level Authentication): authenticates BEFORE desktop session loads — recommended, reduces attack surface. RDP exposed directly on the internet on port 3389 is a primary attack target — require VPN or restrict source IPs. Only available as HOST on Windows Pro and higher (not Home).
Access optical drive on another Mac over the network — used on MacBooks without built-in optical drives.

Enterprise/MSP tool for managing endpoints remotely at scale. Capabilities: remote command execution, script deployment, patch management, monitoring, alerting, inventory, remote console. Examples: ConnectWise Automate, NinjaRMM, Datto RMM. Runs persistent agent on managed endpoints.

Erases device data. Full wipe: factory reset. Selective wipe: corporate data/container only, personal data untouched. Device must be ONLINE to receive command (queues if offline). Cannot be undone. Must be paired with remote backup.

Reinstalls/repairs OS files without deleting user data. "Reset This PC — Keep My Files" in Windows 10/11 performs a repair install — reinstalls Windows, preserves personal files, removes installed applications.

Attempt to reproduce the problem reliably before fixing it. Intermittent issues: document exact conditions (time of day, user action, load level) when it occurs. A problem you cannot reproduce is harder to confirm as fixed.

HD: 1280×720. FHD: 1920×1080 (1080p) — most common. QHD: 2560×1440 (1440p) — sweet spot for gaming. 4K UHD: 3840×2160 — content creation, premium monitors. 8K: 7680×4320 — ultra-premium. PPI (pixels per inch): higher PPI at same screen size = sharper image. Apple Retina = ~220+ PPI where individual pixels indistinguishable at normal viewing distance.

More granular than Task Manager. Five tabs: Overview, CPU, Memory, Disk, Network. Network tab shows per-process TCP connections and remote addresses — useful for identifying processes communicating unexpectedly. Wait chain analysis in CPU tab identifies deadlocked processes.

Best practices for IT professionals using AI: always verify output (AI can be wrong), never enter sensitive or confidential data into public tools, apply human judgment before acting on AI suggestions, use AI as an assistant not a replacement for professional judgment, be transparent about AI use when relevant.
8P8C (8 Position 8 Contact) modular plug. Used for Ethernet (CAT5/5e/6/6a). Crimped onto cable end. RJ-11: 6P2C or 6P4C — telephone lines. RJ-45 is physically larger than RJ-11 and incompatible.

Fake security software displaying alarming (false) infection warnings. Demands payment to "clean" infections that do not exist. May also block legitimate security software from running. Indicators: appeared without user installing it, cannot be closed normally, aggressive popup behavior, demands payment. Fix: boot into Safe Mode, run legitimate malware scanner, remove the rogue program.

Documented, tested steps to undo the change and restore previous state if the change causes problems. Must exist before any change is approved. Good rollback plan: specific, tested, achievable within the maintenance window, identifies who executes it and at what trigger point.

Root/Jailbreak: gaining privileged (superuser/root) access to the device OS, bypassing manufacturer and carrier restrictions. Effects: removes sandboxing between apps, bypasses OS security model, voids warranty, often violates carrier TOS, prevents some banking/enterprise apps from running (SafetyNet/attestation checks). Security risk: malicious apps can gain root access and take full control of device. Enterprise MDM can detect and block enrollment of rooted/jailbroken devices.

Operates at kernel level. Conceals itself and other malware from OS and security tools. Standard AV running inside Windows CANNOT detect it — the OS is compromised and untrustworthy. Detection: boot from external media (WinPE / bootable AV). Removal often requires full OS reinstall.

Layer 3 (Network). Forwards packets between different networks using IP routing tables. Connects subnets, connects LAN to WAN (internet). Makes forwarding decisions based on destination IP address. Maintains routing table: static routes (manually configured) and dynamic routes (learned via routing protocols like OSPF, BGP, RIP). NAT typically runs on router to translate private IPs to public.

Maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. If RPO = 4 hours: backups must run at least every 4 hours, because more than 4 hours of data loss is unacceptable. Drives backup frequency. Set by business requirements, not IT preference.

Maximum acceptable downtime from incident to full service restoration. If RTO = 2 hours: systems must be fully restored within 2 hours of a failure. Drives recovery infrastructure investment (hot standby vs cold standby). Set by business requirements.

Minimal boot — loads only essential Microsoft drivers and services. Types: Safe Mode (no network), Safe Mode with Networking (adds network drivers and services), Safe Mode with Command Prompt (CLI only, no Explorer shell). Used to troubleshoot driver conflicts, remove malware (malware often does not load in Safe Mode). In Windows 10/11, F8 at boot often does not work — use Settings > Recovery > Advanced Startup OR hold Shift while clicking Restart OR run msconfig > Boot tab > Safe boot checkbox.

F8 during boot (legacy, may not work on fast modern systems). Shift+Restart from Start menu → Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Settings → Restart → F4/F5/F6. msconfig > Boot tab > Safe boot checkbox. From WinRE: Troubleshoot → Advanced Options → Startup Settings.

Most malware loads at Windows startup. In Safe Mode, only essential Microsoft drivers and services load — most malware does not run. Scanning in Safe Mode allows anti-malware to detect and remove files that would be locked or actively hiding in normal mode.

F4 — Safe Mode (Minimal): only essential Windows drivers, no networking, no third-party drivers. Useful for driver conflicts. F5 — Safe Mode with Networking: adds network drivers — use when you need internet access to download tools or updates. F6 — Safe Mode with Command Prompt: boots to CLI only, no GUI Explorer shell — for advanced command-line troubleshooting.

SAML: XML standard for auth data exchange across domains. Three parties: Principal (user), Identity Provider (authenticates — e.g. Azure AD), Service Provider (what user accesses — e.g. Salesforce). User authenticates once to IdP → SAML assertion → access to Service Provider without re-auth. SSO: authenticate once, access multiple systems. Reduces password fatigue, centralizes audit logging.

Running untrusted code or files in an isolated environment (VM or container) to observe behavior without risking the host system. Security use case: analyzing suspicious files, testing exploits in safe environment. Browser sandbox: modern browsers sandbox web content from OS.

7-pin data connector (L-shaped, thin). 15-pin power connector (wider L-shape). SATA 3.0 (SATA III): 6 Gbps theoretical (real-world ~550 MB/s). Hot-swap capable on supported controllers. Internal connection: 7-pin data to motherboard SATA port + 15-pin power from PSU.

7-pin SATA data cable: connects drive to motherboard SATA port. Thin, L-shaped connector. 15-pin SATA power cable: from PSU to drive. L-shaped, wider than data. Both are keyed — only insert one way. SATA III max: 6 Gbps.

Flatbed scanner: glass platen, scanning head moves across document. High quality for photos and documents. ADF (Automatic Document Feeder): feeds multiple pages automatically — combined with flatbed in MFP (Multi-Function Printer/Peripheral). Handheld barcode scanner: 1D barcodes (UPC, Code 39) — retail/inventory. 2D scanner: reads QR codes and Data Matrix codes. Signature pad: digitizes handwritten signatures (legal/retail).

Touchscreen unresponsive: soft reset first. Check if screen protector causing issues (especially thick/poor-quality tempered glass). Digitizer failure = hardware repair required. Display cracked: screen function may be retained even with shattered glass — use device until repaired to back up data.

Most to least secure: (1) 3D Facial recognition (Face ID). (2) Fingerprint (balance of security/convenience). (3) PIN — 6-digit minimum (4-digit = only 10,000 combos). (4) Pattern — vulnerable to smudge attacks (oily screen residue reveals the pattern). (5) SWIPE — ZERO SECURITY, only prevents accidental input, never use for business.
Password required after screensaver activation. 5-15 minute timeout. Enforce via GPO. Users: Win+L to manually lock when stepping away.

Scripts can be weaponized by malware (PowerShell is a common malware delivery vector). PowerShell execution policy provides a basic control. Obfuscation: malware often obfuscates PowerShell to evade detection. Never run scripts from untrusted sources. Review scripts before execution. Enterprise environments use application whitelisting (AppLocker) to control which scripts can run.

.bat / .cmd — Windows Batch file (CMD.exe syntax, legacy). .ps1 — PowerShell script (modern Windows automation). .py — Python script (cross-platform, highly versatile). .sh — Bash/Shell script (Linux, macOS, WSL). .vbs — VBScript (legacy Windows automation, mostly replaced by PowerShell). .js — JavaScript (browser-side or Node.js server-side).

Required by OSHA for all hazardous chemicals and materials used in the workplace. Contains: chemical identity, physical properties, health hazards, first aid measures, fire-fighting measures, accidental release measures, handling/storage, exposure controls/PPE, disposal, emergency contact. Technicians must have access to SDS for toner, cleaning chemicals, battery acids, solvents. Formerly called MSDS (Material Safety Data Sheet).
DNS over HTTPS — encrypts DNS queries. Prevents interception and DNS hijacking by network observers. Standard DNS = plaintext UDP port 53. Configure in browser settings or OS.
Multi-pass overwrite. DoD 5220.22-M = 7-pass with defined patterns and verification. Current forensic technology cannot practically recover data after 7 passes. Exam standard reference.

RDP on internet = major attack surface. Best practices: change RDP port from 3389 (obscurity — minor benefit), enable NLA, use VPN + RDP instead of direct RDP exposure, strong passwords and account lockout, limit who can RDP (Remote Desktop Users group). For SSH: disable password auth, use key-only auth, disable root login. Log all remote access sessions.
No single person controls an entire sensitive process. Prevents fraud and reduces insider threat.

Recommended range: 64.4°F–80.6°F (18°C–27.°C). ASHRAE A1 standard commonly cited: 59°F–77°F (15°C–25°C). Exam commonly uses 68°F–77°F as target range. Too hot: thermal throttling, component failure, shortened hardware lifespan, thermal shutdown. Too cold: condensation risk when humidity is also variable. HVAC must be dedicated (not shared with general building) to maintain precise control.

Rack servers use multiple high-speed hot-swap fans (replaceable without powering down). Front-to-rear airflow standard (cold aisle to hot aisle). High-density racks may require rear-door heat exchangers. Data center CRAC (Computer Room Air Conditioning) units provide precision cooling at scale.

Modern replacement for Control Panel. Organized by category: System, Devices, Network, Personalization, Apps, Accounts, Time/Language, Gaming, Ease of Access, Privacy, Update and Security. Microsoft has been migrating settings here from Control Panel since Windows 10.

sfc /scannow — scans all protected Windows system files and replaces corrupted files with cached copies from C:\Windows\System32\dllcache. Requires admin CMD. Cannot repair files that are in use — run from WinRE if needed. Reports results to CBS.log.

sfc /scannow: System File Checker — scans and repairs protected Windows system files from local cache. Run as administrator. Takes 15-30 min. Log: C:\Windows\Logs\CBS\CBS.log. DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth: repairs the Windows component store (the source SFC uses) by downloading clean files from Windows Update — requires internet. Correct sequence: run SFC first → if it can't fix some files → run DISM → run SFC again.
Full Control, Change, Read. Apply ONLY over network share. Sharing tab > Advanced Sharing > Permissions.

Foundational cloud security concept. Provider responsible for: physical security, hypervisor, network infrastructure, hardware — "security of the cloud." Customer responsible for: data, accounts, access management, applications, OS configuration (in IaaS) — "security in the cloud." Responsibility boundary shifts based on service model: IaaS = customer owns most. SaaS = provider owns most.
Visual observation of password entry, PIN, or sensitive screen data. No technical tools needed. Mitigations: privacy screen filters, body positioning, policy about public credential entry.
Reduces media to small fragments (typically ≤1 cm). Effective on ALL media: HDD, SSD, USB, smartphone, optical, tape. Highest assurance — physical medium no longer exists.

Android: installing APKs from outside Google Play Store. Requires enabling "Install unknown apps" (Android 8+) or "Unknown sources" (older Android) — per-app permission in modern Android. Risk: apps from unknown sources not vetted by Google Play Protect. MDM policy can block this setting on managed devices. iOS: sideloading restricted by default — requires Apple Developer account, TestFlight, or enterprise provisioning profile. Jailbreak removes this restriction.
msiexec /i package.msi /quiet /norestart — installs without GUI or reboot prompt. Used in enterprise scripted deployments.

Single channel: one RAM stick (or sticks in a single-channel configuration). Dual channel: two matching sticks running simultaneously — effectively doubles memory bus bandwidth. Install in matching colored slots (check motherboard manual — often slots A2 and B2 for dual channel with 2 sticks). Quad channel: high-end workstation/server platforms (X299, Threadripper, EPYC).

Wireless site survey: maps signal strength and interference across a physical space before or after AP deployment. Tools: Wi-Fi analyzers (NetSpot, Ekahau). Best AP placement: center of coverage area, minimize physical obstructions, use ceiling mount. Multiple APs: use different non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11 on 2.4 GHz) with overlapping coverage for seamless roaming.

Contract between service provider and customer defining: uptime guarantees (e.g., 99.9% = ~8.7 hours downtime/year), response time targets per priority, resolution time targets, penalties for SLA breach, escalation procedures. Measured and reported regularly. Drives ticket prioritization.

Local network: duplex mismatch (force full-duplex on both ends), cable quality issue (damaged cable, wrong CAT for speed needed), switch port running at wrong speed (negotiate to 100Mbps instead of 1Gbps). Wireless: interference, distance from AP, signal obstacles, channel congestion. Internet: ISP bandwidth saturation (run speed test), QoS misconfiguration.

Reads ISO 7816 contact smart cards. Common cards: CAC (Common Access Card — US military/government), PIV (Personal Identity Verification). Used for two-factor authentication (card + PIN). Reader is USB-connected internally.

Self-Monitoring Analysis and Reporting Technology. Built into HDD and SSD firmware. Tracks: reallocated sectors, pending sectors, spin-up time, temperature, power-on hours, uncorrectable errors. View with: CrystalDiskInfo (Windows, free), smartmontools (cross-platform). Status: Good / Caution / Bad. SMART "Caution" or "Bad" = replace drive soon/immediately. SMART is predictive — not all failures are preceded by SMART warning.
SMS/text phishing. Impersonates package delivery, bank, 2FA prompt. Link leads to credential harvesting or malware.

Point-in-time capture of VM state: disk, RAM (optional), and configuration. Taking before risky change (patch, config) = instant rollback if failure. Chain: each snapshot references prior state — long chains degrade performance. NOT a backup: snapshots are stored with VM files on same storage, snapshot deleted when VM deleted. Snapshots are used for change management, not disaster recovery.

Small Outline DIMM. DDR4 SODIMM: 260 pins. DDR5 SODIMM: 262 pins. Install at an angle (~30–45°), press down to lock. Smaller than desktop DIMM. Many modern thin laptops have RAM soldered (LPDDR4/5) — non-upgradeable.

OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer): license tied to specific hardware it shipped with — non-transferable, typically lowest cost. Retail: purchased separately, transferable to another machine (deactivate first), slightly higher cost. Volume/Open License: organization purchases multiple seats under one agreement — corporate deployment. Subscription: recurring payment for time-limited access (Microsoft 365, Adobe Creative Cloud) — software stops working if subscription lapses. FOSS (Free and Open Source Software): free to use, modify, and distribute under open-source license terms (GPL, MIT, Apache, BSD).

Step-by-step documented procedures for routine tasks: how to image a new PC, how to onboard a new user, how to reset an account, how to respond to a specific incident type. Ensures consistency, reduces errors, enables junior staff to perform tasks correctly, required for compliance.

Inspects inbound and outbound email for spam, phishing, and malware. Sits in MX record path. Outbound filtering prevents organization from being blacklisted. URL filtering: blocks malicious links in email. Attachment sandboxing: detonates attachments in isolated environment.
TARGETED phishing using personal details (researched from LinkedIn, corporate sites, breach databases, OSINT). Far more convincing than generic phishing.
System-wide search. Finds files, applications, emails, contacts. Performs calculations and unit conversions. Launch any application by name.
Monitors user activity and transmits data without consent. Browsing habits, credentials, location, personal info.

Malicious SQL in user input fields, passed to database without sanitization. Bypasses authentication (OR '1'='1'), reads/modifies/deletes data. Mitigation: parameterized queries, input validation, WAF.

Flash NAND memory, no moving parts. Much faster than HDD (especially random I/O). Durable (withstands shock). Silent. Lower power. More expensive per GB than HDD. Form factors: 2.5" SATA (drops in to replace HDD), M.2 (small PCB card), PCIe add-in card (enterprise). NAND types: SLC (1 bit/cell, fastest, most durable, most expensive), MLC (2 bit/cell), TLC (3 bit/cell, current mainstream consumer), QLC (4 bit/cell, high density, lower endurance).

No mechanical noise (no moving parts). Drive enters read-only mode (common fail-safe on some SSDs — prevents writes to protect data). Sudden disappearance from system (controller failure). File system corruption without obvious cause. Performance degradation over time (SSD slowdown from full NAND). SMART still provides data: check for reallocated blocks, wear indicator.

Wear-leveling: writes redirected to different physical cells — original data remains in cells that were never overwritten. Multi-pass software wiping NOT reliably effective on SSDs. Use ATA Secure Erase or physical destruction.

Encrypted protocol for remote CLI access to Linux/Unix systems. Port: 22 (TCP). Provides encrypted command-line session — replacement for unencrypted Telnet. Password authentication or key-based authentication. Key-based: client has private key, server has matching public key — more secure than passwords (cannot be guessed, no password to intercept). Common SSH clients: PuTTY (Windows), built-in ssh command (Windows 10+, macOS, Linux).
Disabling hides from casual scans only. Wireless analysis tools detect hidden SSIDs via probe requests. Security through obscurity — not a real control. Supplement to encryption, not substitute.
Clears file allocation table (index) only — actual data NOT overwritten. Recoverable with free tools. NOT a security measure.

Windows 8+: Startup programs managed in Task Manager > Startup tab (replaced MSConfig for this function). MSConfig (System Configuration) still used for boot options (Safe Mode, boot log, base video), services (hide Microsoft services to isolate third-party), and general startup type (Normal/Diagnostic/Selective). Disabling unnecessary startup programs reduces boot time and RAM usage.
Automated tool in WinRE that diagnoses and fixes common boot problems. Try this FIRST before manual bootrec commands. Covers missing/corrupt bootmgr, corrupt BCD, missing system files.

term: Step 1 — Identify and research malware symptoms
definition: Gather information: what symptoms exist, when did they start, what changed recently (new downloads, USB inserted, email clicked). Research the specific malware strain if identifiable. Document current state. This step confirms you are dealing with malware and not hardware/software failure.

Gather information: what are the symptoms? When did it start? What changed recently (updates, new hardware, new software, configuration changes)? Is it affecting one user or many? What error messages appear? Has this worked before? Check event logs. Interview the user — use open-ended questions first, then specific.

Disconnect from all networks: unplug Ethernet, disable Wi-Fi, disable Bluetooth. Prevents: lateral spread to other network devices, C2 (command-and-control) communication, ongoing data exfiltration. Do NOT turn off the computer yet — volatile evidence (running processes, network connections) may be needed.

Apply Occam's Razor — simplest, most likely explanation first. Consider multiple possibilities. "Question the obvious" — check whether device is plugged in, powered on, connected before assuming complex failure. Common causes first (power, cable, driver) before rare causes (hardware failure, firmware bug).

System Restore points may contain malware or malware-modified registry hives. If left enabled, malware can restore itself from a restore point even after removal. Disable via: System Properties > System Protection > Configure > Disable System Protection. Re-enabled in Step 6 AFTER confirmed clean.

Determine if your theory is correct — test it. If confirmed: proceed to step 4. If not confirmed: establish a new theory and test it (return to step 2). Testing: swap components, check settings, reproduce in controlled way. Confirm root cause before proceeding to fix.

Actual removal process: (a) Boot into Safe Mode (malware often does not load in Safe Mode). (b) Update anti-malware definitions (may require temporarily restoring network if offline, or using another device). (c) Run full anti-malware scan. (d) Quarantine and remove detected threats. (e) Manually remove remaining malware: delete malicious files, remove registry run entries, remove malicious services, restore hosts file. (f) If malware cannot be fully removed — reimage the machine.

Once cause is confirmed, plan the fix: document planned steps, consider impact on users, identify rollback path if fix fails, get authorization if required (change management). Implement the solution systematically.

term: Step 5 — Schedule scans and run updates
definition: After removal: schedule recurring malware scans. Run Windows Update to patch all vulnerabilities that may have been exploited. Update all software (browsers, Java, Office). Update anti-malware definitions. Verify Windows Defender and Windows Update are functioning.

After fix: confirm the original problem is resolved — have user verify if possible. Check for related issues caused by the fix. Implement preventive measures: update drivers, apply patches, document the fix, schedule regular maintenance.

term: Step 6 — Enable System Restore and create restore point
definition: Re-enable System Restore (System Properties > System Protection > Configure > Turn on). Immediately create a new restore point to capture the clean state. This clean restore point becomes the recovery baseline going forward.

Record everything: symptoms observed, theories tested, root cause identified, solution implemented, steps taken, time spent, outcome. Feeds knowledge base for future incidents. Required for compliance. Enables faster resolution of repeat issues.

Train the user on how the infection occurred and how to prevent recurrence: avoid clicking email links/attachments from unknown senders, download software only from official sources, recognize phishing, keep software updated, use strong unique passwords. Goal: reduce the likelihood of reinfection.

term: Step 8 — Document findings, actions, and outcomes
definition: Record: what malware was found, how it was identified, what steps were taken, what tools were used, what the result was. Documentation feeds the knowledge base for future incidents. Required for compliance environments. May be required for legal/forensic purposes in breach situations.
Quarantine (2) before remediation. Disable System Restore (3) before scanning. Re-enable System Restore (9) AFTER confirmed clean. Educate user (10) is ALWAYS last.

2.5" SATA SSD: replaces 2.5" HDD directly (same connector and form factor). M.2 NVMe SSD: M.2 slot on motherboard — most laptops have one M.2 slot (2280 size most common). Migration: clone existing drive to new drive using software (Macrium Reflect, Clonezilla) before swapping, or do fresh OS install.

Straight-through: same wiring standard (T568B–T568B) both ends. Used for: PC to switch, PC to router, switch uplink to router. Crossover: T568A one end, T568B other. Used for: switch to switch, hub to hub, PC to PC direct (largely obsolete — modern switches use auto-MDIX to auto-detect and adjust).

32-bit mask that identifies network vs host bits. Written in dotted decimal (255.255.255.0) or CIDR prefix notation (/24). /24 = 24 network bits = 255.255.255.0. Each subnet: 2^(host bits) addresses total. Subtract 2 for usable hosts (network address and broadcast address not assignable). /24: 256 addresses, 254 usable hosts. /25: 128 addresses, 126 usable. /16: 65,536 addresses, 65,534 usable. /8: 16,777,216 addresses.

sudo: preferred — execute one command with elevated privileges using YOUR own password. Logs all commands. su: switch to another user session (usually root) using THAT user's password. Persistent elevated session with no per-command logging — less preferred. Never use su root if sudo is available.
Compromise vendor/manufacturer to inject malicious code/components into software or hardware supply chain. Propagates to all customers. SolarWinds = prominent real-world example.

Surge protector: absorbs voltage spikes/surges only — does NOT provide battery backup. If power fails, equipment shuts off immediately. UPS: provides battery backup AND surge protection. For servers and critical equipment: always use UPS, not just surge protector. MOV (Metal Oxide Varistor) is the component in surge protectors that absorbs spikes — degrades over time and must be replaced.

Layer 2 (Data Link). Learns MAC addresses and associates them with ports in a MAC address table (CAM table). Forwards frames ONLY to the destination port — not all ports. Each port is its own collision domain. Benefits over hub: full-duplex operation per port, dedicated bandwidth per port, no collisions between ports. Managed switch: configurable (VLANs, STP, port security, QoS, LACP). Unmanaged: plug-and-play.

Physical swelling/puffing of Li-ion battery cell due to gas buildup from cell degradation. SAFETY EMERGENCY: swollen battery is a fire and explosion risk. Immediate actions: stop charging, do not drop or puncture, remove from device if safely possible (may require opening device), do not store near flammables, take to battery recycling/hazmat disposal. Device may feel thicker or back cover pops up. Never continue using a swollen battery.

Creates a new full backup by combining the last full backup with subsequent incremental backups — without reading the original data source again. Reduces backup window impact on production systems. Modern backup software feature.

Centralized log collection. Syslog protocol: port 514 UDP (or TCP for reliable delivery). Network devices, servers, and applications send log messages to central syslog server for: correlation, alerting, compliance, forensics. SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) extends syslog with automated correlation and alerting.

Startup and boot configuration. General tab: Normal, Diagnostic (minimal services), or Selective startup. Boot tab: Safe Boot options (Minimal, Network, Command Prompt), boot log (ntbtlog.txt), timeout for multi-OS, processor/memory limits for diagnostics. Services tab: enable/disable individual services — "Hide all Microsoft services" to isolate third-party services. Startup tab (legacy — now in Task Manager). Diagnostic startup troubleshooting: enable Diagnostic → confirm problem disappears → re-enable services one at a time to isolate culprit.

Read-only reporting tool. Comprehensive snapshot: OS version, processor, BIOS version, installed RAM, hardware components, installed drivers, running services, environment variables. Cannot make changes. Can export to text file. Use for documentation and compatibility verification.

Security feature that prevents modification of /System directory even by root or administrators. Requires booting into Recovery Mode to disable (not recommended). Protects core OS files from malware and accidental modification.

Before installing any application: verify CPU (speed, core count, specific instruction sets), RAM (available — not just total installed), storage space (plus temp space during install), GPU (dedicated vs integrated — professional apps, gaming), OS version/edition compatibility.

Rolls back registry and system files to a previously saved restore point. Does NOT affect user data (documents, photos, downloads) — only system files and registry. Access from: System Properties > System Protection > System Restore, or from WinRE. Use when: OS instability, failed driver install, bad system change.

systemctl start service: starts immediately. systemctl stop service: stops immediately. systemctl restart service: stops then starts. systemctl status service: shows current state and recent log. systemctl enable service: configures auto-start at boot. systemctl disable service: removes auto-start. systemctl is-active service: check if running.

Both define the pin-to-wire-color mapping for RJ-45 termination. T568B (most common in US): white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown. T568A: white-green, green, white-orange, blue, white-blue, orange, white-brown, brown. Consistent use of either standard within a building is fine — mixing causes problems. Straight-through cable: same standard (T568B–T568B) on both ends — PC to switch/router. Crossover cable: different standards (T568A–T568B) — switch to switch or hub to hub (mostly obsolete with auto-MDIX).

Cisco-developed AAA protocol. Used for NETWORK DEVICE management authentication (routers, switches, firewalls) — NOT for wireless clients. TCP port 49. Separates AAA into independent steps. Encrypts the ENTIRE packet payload. Supports granular command-level authorization. Preferred for network device administration in Cisco environments.

Unauthorized person follows authorized through secured entry WITHOUT their knowledge. Piggybacking: same but WITH their knowledge (held door). Both bypass physical controls. Mitigation: access control vestibule.

Tailgating: unauthorized person follows authorized person through secured entry WITHOUT the authorized person's knowledge. Piggybacking: same action but WITH the authorized person's knowledge and consent (they held the door). Both bypass physical access controls. Mitigation: access control vestibule (mantrap).

Processes tab: all running apps and background processes with real-time CPU, RAM, disk, network, GPU — right-click to End Task, open file location, or set priority. Performance tab: real-time resource graphs (CPU speed/utilization, memory, disk, network, GPU, uptime) — click "Open Resource Monitor" for more detail. Startup tab: CRITICAL — lists all startup programs with High/Medium/Low startup impact rating — right-click to Disable startup items; controls user-level apps only (not Windows services). Users tab: active sessions with resource use — admins can disconnect/sign out users. Services tab: list of Windows services with status — can start/stop/restart, opens services.msc.

Automates scripts/programs based on triggers. Time-based (run at 2 AM daily) or event-based (user login, specific event). Tasks can run whether user is logged in or not, and with elevated privileges. Common uses: automated backups, maintenance scripts, log rotation.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): connection-oriented. Three-way handshake before data (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK). Guarantees ordered, reliable, error-checked delivery. Slower due to overhead. Used where data integrity is critical: web, email, file transfer. UDP (User Datagram Protocol): connectionless. No handshake, no guaranteed delivery, no ordering. Faster, lower overhead. Used where speed matters more than reliability: streaming, VoIP, DNS queries, DHCP, gaming.

Maximum sustained heat output in watts — cooler must be rated to dissipate at least this much. Consumer CPUs: 65W–125W typical. HEDT/server: 250W+. Low-power (laptop/embedded): 15W–45W. Does not equal power consumption — actual consumption varies with load.

Third-party remote support tools. Both use cloud relay servers — outbound connections only from both endpoints. No port forwarding or firewall rules needed on either side. Works through NAT and firewalls. Unattended access mode allows connection without user present (requires pre-configuration). Commonly used for remote IT support and managed service providers. Session is encrypted.

Legacy unencrypted remote CLI protocol. Port: 23 (TCP). All data including credentials transmitted in plaintext — easily intercepted. NEVER use on untrusted networks. Replaced by SSH. Still appears in exam context — always wrong answer when security matters. Some network devices (older switches/routers) may still use it on internal management networks.

Located: /Applications/Utilities. CLI access to underlying Unix system. Supports Bash and Zsh shells. Common commands: ls, cd, sudo, chmod, top, man. macOS equivalent of Windows Command Prompt/PowerShell.

A backup that has never been tested is not a backup — it is an assumption. Regular restore tests confirm backup integrity and validate recovery procedures. Test schedule should match business criticality. Document test results.

CPUs and GPUs generate significant heat — typically 65–300W TDP (Thermal Design Power). Without adequate cooling: thermal throttling (CPU/GPU reduces clock speed to lower heat), system instability, accelerated component degradation, thermal shutdown. High ambient temperature amplifies cooling challenges.

Thermal Interface Material fills microscopic air gaps between CPU surface and cooler base. Air = poor heat conductor. Thermal paste = better conductor, dramatically improves heat transfer. Application: pea-sized amount in center of CPU die. Spreads evenly under cooler pressure. Too much = can insulate or spill on socket. Too little = hot spots. Old/dried thermal paste must be replaced — symptom: unexplained high temperatures on previously functioning system.

Heat-sensitive paper (thermal paper) — no ink or toner. Print head applies heat to paper, activating thermal dye. Paper turns dark in heated areas. Receipt printers, shipping labels, barcode labels, point-of-sale. Thermal transfer: uses heat to transfer ink from ribbon to paper/label — more durable, used for barcodes. Direct thermal (no ribbon): cheaper, paper yellows/fades with heat/light exposure.

Wrong side of paper loaded: thermal paper has coated and uncoated sides — coated side faces print head. Loading the wrong side = blank output. Paper yellowing/fading: thermal paper degrades with heat, UV light, or certain chemicals. Use correct thermal paper grade. Head dirty: clean with IPA swab.

Intel standard. TB1/TB2 use Mini DisplayPort connector. TB3/TB4 use USB-C connector. TB3/TB4 bandwidth: 40 Gbps (vs USB 3.2 Gen 2 at 10 Gbps). Supports: PCIe tunneling (connect external GPU), DisplayPort (video), USB, power delivery. Daisy-chain up to 6 TB devices. TB4 requires Thunderbolt certification; not all USB-C ports are Thunderbolt. Identifies by lightning bolt icon next to port.

TB1: 10 Gbps, Mini DisplayPort connector. TB2: 20 Gbps, Mini DisplayPort connector. TB3: 40 Gbps, USB-C connector, also supports USB 3.1, DisplayPort 1.2, PCIe x4. TB4: 40 Gbps, USB-C connector, mandates minimum specs (display support, charging, PCIe bandwidth). Intel standard — not all USB-C is Thunderbolt (look for lightning bolt icon).

Native backup utility. Automatic incremental snapshots: hourly (past 24 hours), daily (past month), weekly (older data). Requires external drive or network storage. Restores entire system or individual files. macOS equivalent of Windows Backup with versioning.
Retained in WPA2 only for backward compatibility with legacy devices. Has known vulnerabilities. Deprecated. Degrades security of entire network segment if used.

Toner cartridges: many manufacturers have take-back programs (HP, Canon, Brother). Third-party recycling drop-offs. Ink cartridges: similar take-back programs. Do not shred or crush toner cartridges (toner dispersal hazard).

Two-part tool: tone generator injects an audio signal (tone) into a cable. Inductive probe detects the tone through walls, ceilings, in bundles. Used to trace cable runs from outlet to patch panel. Essential for identifying unlabeled cables. Also called fox-and-hound.

Time-based One-Time Password. Generated using current time + shared secret. Valid ~30 seconds. Server and app synchronized to same time source. Used in Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Authy.

Capacitive overlay on standard monitor. Uses USB for touch data, video connection for display. Multi-touch support: pinch-to-zoom, rotate gestures. Touch accuracy depends on digitizer quality and calibration. Calibrate via Windows Tablet PC Settings if touch is misregistered.

Built-in pointing device — ClickPad style (no discrete buttons, entire pad is clickable). Connects via ribbon cable and ZIF connector. Driver-controlled sensitivity and gesture support. Can be disabled in BIOS/UEFI or via Fn key. Replaced as a unit.

Digitizer layer bonded over LCD panel. Capacitive touch (modern) — detects electrical field disturbance from finger. Stylus support: active stylus uses battery and tip sensor for pressure sensitivity (Microsoft Surface Pen, Apple Pencil). Gorilla Glass or similar cover glass for scratch resistance.

Traces packet path hop-by-hop to destination. Uses TTL manipulation — starts with TTL=1, increments by 1 per probe. Each router decrements TTL by 1; when TTL=0, router returns "Time Exceeded" ICMP message — revealing its IP. Shows per-hop RTT. Identifies where routing breaks (timeout * at specific hop). Useful for identifying network congestion and routing issues.
Signature-based — compares files against known malware database. Effective against known threats. Blind to zero-days, novel variants, and fileless malware. Requires continuous definition updates.
Disguised as legitimate software. User installs willingly. Executes payload (backdoor, keylogger, dropper). DOES NOT SELF-REPLICATE — relies on social engineering.
AP schedules when devices wake to transmit/receive — IoT and battery-powered devices can sleep longer. Dramatically extends battery life for IoT sensors, smartwatches, and mobile devices.

Runs directly on physical hardware — no host OS. Best performance (near-native). Used in production servers and data centers. Examples: VMware ESXi (vSphere), Microsoft Hyper-V Server (standalone, not the Windows role), Citrix XenServer, KVM (built into Linux kernel). Managed via separate management console/VM (vCenter for ESXi, Hyper-V Manager).

Runs as application on top of host OS (Windows, macOS, Linux). Less efficient — extra OS layer adds overhead. Used on workstations, laptops, for development/testing. Examples: VMware Workstation, Oracle VirtualBox (free, cross-platform), Parallels Desktop (macOS).

User Account Control — elevation request mechanism. Secure desktop: dims screen, runs prompt in isolated session — prevents auto-click. Standard user: must provide ADMIN credentials. Administrator: sees confirmation prompt (not credential request) under default settings.
1 (Always notify): prompts ALL changes. 2 (Default): only when apps request changes. 3: same as 2, no secure desktop dimming. 4 (Never notify): disables UAC — not recommended.

Credentials leaked via malicious app, phishing, or data breach used to access other accounts (credential stuffing). Signs: unexpected login notifications, unfamiliar activity in accounts, unexpected charges. Response: change compromised passwords, enable MFA on all accounts, review app permissions.

New user accounts appearing in Local Users and Groups (lusrmgr.msc) or on login screen that were not created by IT — sign of compromise or malware creating backdoor accounts. Investigate and remove unauthorized accounts. Change all admin passwords.

Malware installs rogue proxy to route all HTTP/HTTPS traffic through attacker server for interception. Symptom: browser redirects, slow browsing, unexpected certificate warnings. Check: Internet Options (inetcpl.cpl) > Connections > LAN Settings — remove unauthorized proxy.
Universal Naming Convention. Format: \\servername\sharename or \\servername\sharename\subfolder. Can use IP: \\192.168.1.50\shared. Use in File Explorer address bar or Run dialog (Win+R).

Device may auto-connect to previously known networks — attacker can set up evil twin AP with same SSID. Bluetooth devices may connect automatically if previously paired. Mitigation: configure known network priorities, disable auto-connect to open networks, keep Bluetooth off when not in use.

In-place upgrade: Home → Pro (via product key in Settings), Pro → Enterprise (in-place). Windows 10 → Windows 11 in-place if hardware meets requirements. Enterprise CANNOT be downgraded to Pro in-place — requires clean install.

Home → Pro: in-place via product key. Pro → Enterprise: in-place. Enterprise → Pro: REQUIRES clean install (cannot downgrade in-place). Pre-upgrade checklist: verify hardware compatibility (PC Health Check for Win11), back up all data, verify app/driver compatibility, verify network drivers available.

Battery backup that provides clean, conditioned power during outages. Online UPS: always runs through inverter — provides best power conditioning. Offline/Standby UPS: switches to battery when outage detected (brief switchover delay). Line-interactive UPS: handles voltage fluctuations without switching to battery (most common for IT). Sized in VA (volt-amperes) — must exceed total connected load. Runtime = time on battery before shutdown.

Type-A: rectangular, standard host-side connector. Type-B: square/trapezoidal device-side connector. Mini-USB: older small devices (cameras, some phones). Micro-USB: small devices, older Android phones. Type-C: reversible, oval, modern standard — supports USB, Thunderbolt, DisplayPort, power delivery. USB 2.0: 480 Mbps. USB 3.0 (3.1 Gen 1): 5 Gbps, blue ports/connectors. USB 3.1 Gen 2 (3.2 Gen 2): 10 Gbps. USB 3.2 Gen 2x2: 20 Gbps. USB4: 40 Gbps (uses USB-C).

All-in-one security appliance combining: firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus/anti-malware, content filtering, VPN, DLP. Single device, easier management. Trade-off: single point of failure for all security functions. Common in SMB environments.

UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair): standard CAT cable — no metallic shielding. Relies on twist rate for EMI rejection. Less expensive, flexible. STP (Shielded Twisted Pair): foil or braid shielding around pairs or bundle. Better EMI resistance for electrically noisy environments (factory floors near motors). More expensive, harder to terminate, requires grounded connectors.

Windows Batch: %variable% syntax (e.g., %USERNAME% for current user). PowerShell: $variable syntax (e.g., $env:USERNAME). Bash: $variable syntax (e.g., $USER). Python: variable syntax without sigil (e.g., username = "Jordan"). Environment variables exist pre-defined by the OS and are accessible in all script types.

Desktop OS (Windows, Linux) hosted on centralized server in data center or cloud. Users access via thin client, web browser, or RDP client. Benefits: centralized management, consistent environment, data stays in data center (no sensitive data on endpoint), easy disaster recovery. Thin client: low-power endpoint device — just enough hardware to display the remote desktop.

VGA (DB-15): analog, legacy, no audio, 15-pin D-sub connector. Requires active adapter to convert from digital GPU output. DVI: Digital Visual Interface. DVI-D (digital only), DVI-A (analog only), DVI-I (both). Single-link vs dual-link. Legacy on modern systems. HDMI: digital audio + video. Type A (full size), Type C (mini), Type D (micro). Versions: 1.4 (4K@30Hz), 2.0 (4K@60Hz, 18 Gbps), 2.1 (4K@120Hz, 8K@60Hz, 48 Gbps). DisplayPort: high-bandwidth digital A/V. DP 1.4: 32.4 Gbps, supports 4K@120Hz, 8K@60Hz. Supports MST (daisy-chaining multiple monitors). Mini DisplayPort: same signal, smaller connector (used in older MacBooks and some ultrabooks).

VGA: analog, DB-15, 15 pins in 3 rows, no audio. Legacy — replaced in most modern monitors. DVI: digital (DVI-D), analog+digital (DVI-I), analog only (DVI-A). Single-link (max 1920×1200@60Hz) vs dual-link (max 2560×1600@60Hz). HDMI: all-digital audio+video. Most universal. Versions 1.4, 2.0, 2.1 (see 2.7). DisplayPort: highest bandwidth standard display connector. Supports DSC (Display Stream Compression) for very high resolutions/refresh rates. MST (Multi-Stream Transport): daisy-chain multiple monitors from one DP port. USB-C/Thunderbolt: single-cable video + data + power.

Closed Circuit Television cameras at entrances, corridors, sensitive areas. Serves both deterrence (visible cameras discourage misconduct) and post-incident review. IP cameras allow network-based monitoring and recording.
Functioning camera, microphone, audio output. Bandwidth: 1-4 Mbps per participant for video. Firewall rules may need adjustment for specific ports. Recording permissions controlled by admin.

Complete emulated computer running on a hypervisor. Contains: virtual CPU (vCPU), virtual RAM, virtual storage (VMDK for VMware, VHD/VHDX for Hyper-V), virtual NIC(s). Isolated from host and other VMs — a crash or compromise of one VM does not affect others (unless hypervisor vulnerability). Each VM has its own OS instance.

Windows uses disk space as overflow when physical RAM is full. Pagefile.sys at root of C:. Dramatically slower than physical RAM (disk vs RAM speed). Excessive paging = performance degradation. 32-bit OS hard cap: 4 GB RAM maximum regardless of physical RAM installed. 64-bit OS: practical cap is motherboard/CPU specification (2 TB+ in high-end systems).

VT-x (Intel Virtualization Technology) / AMD-V: hardware virtualization extensions enabling Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors. Must be enabled in BIOS/UEFI. All modern CPUs support it but it may be disabled by default in some OEM systems. VT-d (Intel) / AMD-Vi: I/O virtualization (PCIe passthrough to VMs — GPU passthrough).

Self-replicating, requires a HOST FILE. Attaches to executable/document. Runs when infected file executed, copies to other files. Boot sector virus targets MBR — loads before OS, very difficult to detect from within Windows.
Voice phishing via phone call. Impersonates IT support, financial institution, government. Extracts credentials or directs victim to install remote access software.

Logical network segmentation on a managed switch — separates traffic into isolated broadcast domains without requiring separate physical switches. Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without routing (inter-VLAN routing via router or Layer 3 switch). Common use: separate HR, finance, guest, IoT networks on same physical infrastructure. Trunk port: carries multiple VLANs between switches (802.1Q tagging). Access port: carries single VLAN to end device.

Hardware consolidation: run many VMs on one physical server (better hardware utilization). Isolation: VMs separated from each other and host. Snapshots: save VM state at a point in time — instantly revert if something goes wrong. Cloning: duplicate a VM for rapid deployment (template → deploy). Live migration: move running VM between physical hosts with no downtime (vMotion in VMware). Test environments: safe sandbox for testing without risking production.

VM: full OS per instance, stronger isolation, more resource overhead, slower startup. Container: shared kernel, weaker isolation, minimal overhead, nearly instant startup. VMs for: different OS requirements, strong security isolation. Containers for: app portability, microservices, fast deployment.

Cross-platform remote desktop protocol. Default port: 5900 (TCP). NOT encrypted by default — must tunnel through SSH for security. Open standard with many implementations (RealVNC, TigerVNC, UltraVNC). Platform-independent — Windows, Linux, macOS. Commonly used in environments where RDP is unavailable (Linux desktops).

Assess user's technical level and adjust language accordingly. Non-technical users: avoid jargon, use analogies, plain language. Technical users: appropriate technical terms are fine. Using jargon with non-technical users causes confusion and frustration — does not demonstrate competence, it hinders communication.

Settings > Network and Internet > VPN. Add a VPN connection specifying: VPN provider, server address, VPN type (PPTP/L2TP/IKEv2/SSTP). VPN encrypts traffic between client and VPN server. Used to securely access corporate resources remotely. IKEv2: most modern, fast reconnect. SSTP: uses HTTPS (port 443) — bypasses most firewalls. L2TP/IPSec: common, uses port 1701 + 500 + 4500. PPTP: legacy, weak encryption — avoid.

Total system power draw = sum of all components. GPU is typically the largest consumer (100W–350W+). CPU: 65W–125W typical. Factor in expansion and future upgrades. Rule of thumb: target 80% of PSU capacity under peak load (a 750W system peaks at 600W → 750W PSU). Overpowering = efficient and runs cooler. Under-powering = instability, component damage, PSU failure.

Hosts HTTP/HTTPS content. Listens on port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS). Software: Apache, Nginx, IIS (Windows). Serves HTML, CSS, JS, images, and web application content. TLS certificate required for HTTPS.

External USB webcam: plug-and-play. Built-in laptop webcam: USB internally. Features: resolution (1080p, 4K), frame rate (30/60fps), autofocus, low-light performance, built-in microphone, privacy shutter. Used for: video conferencing, streaming, security monitoring.

Webcam: typically built into display bezel, connected via USB or proprietary flat cable routed through hinge. IR camera: supports Windows Hello facial recognition — uses infrared illumination, works in the dark. Microphone: built into bezel or palmrest — often array microphone (multiple elements for noise cancellation).

BROKEN — never use. RC4 cipher implementation has fundamental weaknesses. Key crackable by capturing sufficient packets in minutes with modern tools. If WEP appears as an answer option, it is always wrong.
Spear phishing targeting EXECUTIVES (CEO, CFO, board). Also called Business Email Compromise (BEC) when targeting financial transactions. High-value targets.

Scans 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands for SSIDs, signal strength (dBm), channel usage, noise level, connected clients. Used for: AP placement optimization, channel selection (avoid co-channel interference), detecting rogue APs, troubleshooting poor wireless performance. Mobile apps (Wi-Fi Analyzer on Android) or dedicated hardware.

802.11 wireless networking — primary data connection for most mobile devices. 2.4 GHz (longer range, more interference) vs 5 GHz (shorter range, less congestion, faster). Modern devices support dual-band or tri-band (adding 6 GHz for Wi-Fi 6E). See Domain 2 for full 802.11 standard details.

Windows 10 available in both 32-bit and 64-bit. Windows 11 is 64-bit ONLY — no 32-bit version exists. Windows 11 also requires TPM 2.0, UEFI with Secure Boot, 64-bit CPU (1 GHz+, 2+ cores), 4 GB RAM minimum, 64 GB storage minimum, and DirectX 12 compatible graphics.

Built-in endpoint protection in Windows 10/11. Real-time protection + behavioral monitoring. Definitions updated via Windows Update. Access: Settings > Privacy and Security > Windows Security. Quarantine, exclusions, manual scan available. Third-party AV disables Defender automatically when installed.

Enterprise-equivalent feature set licensed specifically for academic institutions (schools, colleges, universities). Available only through volume licensing with educational institutions. Windows Pro Education mirrors Pro for academic environments.

Everything in Pro/Pro for Workstations PLUS four exclusive features: (1) App-V (Application Virtualization — sandboxed app execution without traditional install). (2) UE-V (User Environment Virtualization — syncs per-user app settings across domain machines). (3) DirectAccess (always-on, automatic VPN-less encrypted corporate connectivity). (4) Credential Guard (virtualization-based security isolates credential hashes from OS — even kernel-level compromise cannot extract stored creds). Volume licensing ONLY — no OEM, no Retail purchase path. Max RAM: 6 TB, up to 4 CPUs.

Domain (AD network, least restrictive). Private (trusted/home network, moderate). Public (unknown network, MOST RESTRICTIVE, default for new connections). Each profile configured independently via wf.msc.
Consumer features: basic Windows features, Microsoft Store, Windows Defender AV, Windows Firewall, basic local accounts, workgroup networking. OEM or Retail licensing.

Four critical missing features: (1) NO BitLocker full-disk encryption. (2) NO Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc does not exist). (3) NO domain join — cannot connect to Active Directory. (4) NO Remote Desktop HOST — cannot accept incoming RDP connections. Home CAN use RDP as a client (to connect out) — it just cannot host. Max RAM support: 128 GB (64-bit).

Adds all four features Home lacks: BitLocker, gpedit.msc (Group Policy Editor), Active Directory domain join, Remote Desktop hosting (accepting inbound RDP). Also adds: Windows Information Protection (WIP), Hyper-V virtualization, Assigned Access (kiosk mode), Remote Desktop client + host. Max RAM: 2 TB (64-bit). Available OEM, Retail, or Volume licensing.

Everything in Pro PLUS: ReFS (Resilient File System) support as a local drive option, persistent memory (NVDIMM) support, up to 4 physical CPUs, up to 6 TB RAM. Designed for high-performance scientific, 3D rendering, financial simulation workloads. Not for standard business use.

Malware commonly disables Windows Defender and Windows Update to prevent detection and removal. Symptoms: Defender shows "turned off by group policy" or cannot be enabled, Windows Update returns errors. Certain rootkits or advanced malware specifically target security services. Indicator of serious infection requiring Safe Mode remediation.

Run Windows Update Troubleshooter. Restart BITS (Background Intelligent Transfer Service) and wuauserv services. Reset Software Distribution folder: stop wuauserv, rename C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution to SoftwareDistribution.old, restart wuauserv. Check that malware is not blocking updates. Boot to Safe Mode and attempt update.

Accessed by: booting from Windows installation media and selecting "Repair your computer," or from Advanced startup options. Tools available: Startup Repair (automated boot issue detection and fix), System Restore (roll back to restore point), System Image Recovery (restore from full image backup), Command Prompt (bootrec, sfc, diskpart, etc.), Uninstall Updates, Startup Settings (Safe Mode options).

Startup Repair — automatically diagnoses and fixes common boot issues. System Restore — reverts Windows to a previous restore point (does NOT affect user data). System Image Recovery — restores full system image backup. Command Prompt — manual repair via CLI. Reset this PC — reinstall Windows keeping or removing user files. Uninstall Updates — remove recent update causing instability.

Extends wired network to wireless clients. Operates at Layer 2 — bridges wireless and wired segments. SSID broadcast, WPA3/WPA2 security. Fat AP (standalone) vs thin AP (managed by wireless controller). Placement: central to coverage area, minimize walls/obstacles, use multiple APs for large areas with roaming (same SSID, different channels).

Mini PCIe or M.2 A/E key wireless card. Located under bottom panel, often under a small cover. Connects via M.2 or mini PCIe slot. Two antenna cables (main and aux, often labelled 1 and 2 or black and white) attach to the card with push-on connectors. Antenna wires route through display bezel — must be rerouted if replacing display.

WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy): broken and obsolete. RC4 cipher with weak IV implementation — cracked in minutes. Never use. WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access): TKIP cipher, patch for WEP hardware — weak, deprecated. WPA2: AES-CCMP cipher — current minimum standard for all deployments. WPA3: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces PSK handshake — resistant to offline dictionary attacks (KRACK vulnerability fixed).

Weak signal: AP placement too far, obstacles (concrete walls, metal), check dBm reading in Wi-Fi settings (closer to 0 is stronger, e.g., -50 dBm excellent, -80 dBm poor). Wrong SSID/passphrase: forget network and rejoin. Incorrect security type: mismatch between AP security setting and client. IP configuration issue: even with Wi-Fi connected, may have IP issue — check ipconfig.

Network protocol analyzer (packet capture). Captures all traffic on a network interface. Filters: display filter (ip.addr==192.168.1.1, tcp.port==80, http). Follow TCP stream: reassembles entire conversation. Used for: deep protocol troubleshooting, security analysis, verifying encryption, examining DHCP/DNS conversations. Requires appropriate permissions and authorization.

Peer-to-peer networking. Each machine maintains its own local user account database. To access another machine's resources, a local account must exist on that machine for the accessing user. No centralized management or Group Policy. No Single Sign-On. Practical for fewer than ~20 machines. Windows Home supports workgroups. All Windows editions support workgroups.
Self-replicating WITHOUT needing a host file. Spreads autonomously across networks exploiting vulnerabilities. No user action needed after initial infection.
Interim fix for WEP using TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol). Deprecated. Known vulnerabilities. Do not use for new deployments.

Individual user credentials via RADIUS server — no shared key. Each user authenticates with username/password, certificate, or smart card. AP (authenticator) forwards credentials to RADIUS. Each user session gets unique encryption keys. Compromise of one user does not affect others. Required in corporate environments.

Pre-Shared Key — one password shared by all users. Uses AES-CCMP cipher (strong). Weakness: if PSK compromised, all traffic can potentially be decrypted. Suitable for home and SOHO. Minimum passphrase: 8 characters.

Personal (PSK): single pre-shared key for all users. Simple, suitable for home/SOHO. All users share same key — key compromise = change key on all devices. Enterprise (802.1X): individual credentials per user, authenticated via RADIUS server. User gets unique key per session. Certificate-based auth possible. Centralized user management. Required for organizations that need per-user accountability.
192-bit security mode with stronger algorithms. For high-security government and financial deployments.

SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces WPA2 PSK four-way handshake. WPA2 PSK handshake can be captured and brute-forced offline — SAE requires active AP interaction per guess (rate limiting possible), making offline attacks infeasible. Forward secrecy: session keys safe even if password is discovered later. OWE: unique per-device encryption keys.
WPA3-SAE preferred. WPA2-AES minimum acceptable. Never WEP or WPA-TKIP.

x86 (32-bit): original PC architecture, supports max 4 GB RAM. x64 (64-bit, also called AMD64 or Intel 64): backward compatible with x86, supports massive RAM and 64-bit apps. All modern desktop/laptop CPUs are x64. ARM: RISC architecture — used in mobile devices (iOS, Android), Apple M-series chips, Raspberry Pi. More energy efficient per operation than x86. Windows ARM runs on Qualcomm Snapdragon Surface devices.
Extended Detection and Response. Correlates telemetry across endpoints, network, email, cloud, and identity. Sees full attack chain across entire environment.
High-performance journaling filesystem for enterprise Linux. Max volume and file: 8 exabytes. Used where performance and scalability are prioritized.
Malicious JavaScript injected into web content. Executes in victim's browser — steals cookies, session tokens, credentials. Targets USERS (unlike SQL injection which targets the database).
Unknown to vendor at time of exploitation. No patch exists. Cannot be remediated by standard patch management. Mitigations: layered defense, EDR behavioral detection, network segmentation.

Zero Insertion Force connectors secure flat ribbon cables (keyboard, touchpad, webcam, display). Locking mechanism: small brown or black tab flips up 90° to release. Cable slides in/out with zero force when unlocked. Forcing a locked ZIF connector tears the cable or destroys the connector — this is the most common laptop repair mistake.
A policy that governs employees' use of company equipment and Internet services. ISPs may also apply AUPs to their customers.
An authentication mechanism that allows a user to present a smart card to operate an entry system.
The collection of access control entries (ACEs) that determines which subjects (user accounts, host IP addresses, etc.) are allowed or denied access to the object and the privileges given.
A secure entry system with two gateways, only one of which is open at any one time.
A device that provides a connection between wireless devices and can connect to wired networks, implementing an infrastructure mode WLAN.
Policy that prevents access to an account under certain conditions, such as excessive failed authentication attempts.
A set of rules governing user security information, such as password expiration and uniqueness, set globally.
Tracking authorized usage of a resource or use of rights by a subject and alerting when unauthorized use is detected or attempted.
Policies and processes that ensure asset and service purchases/contracts are fully managed, secure, use authorized suppliers/vendors, and meet business goals.
Penetration testing techniques that interact with target systems directly.
Detective/preventive controls that use an agent or network configuration to monitor hosts, allowing accurate credentialed scanning but consuming host resources and detectable by threat actors.
A wireless network where connected devices communicate directly with each other instead of over an established medium.
Broadcast mechanism matching a hardware MAC address to an IP address on a local network segment.
An attacker's ability to obtain, maintain, and diversify access to network systems using exploits and malware.
Software that records information about a PC and its user, typically with acknowledged consent.
High-performance symmetric encryption mode providing authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD).
A type of network isolation that physically separates a host from other hosts or a network from all other networks.
Adjusting detection/correlation rules to reduce false positives and low-priority alerts.
Operations that transform plaintext into ciphertext with cryptographic properties (a cipher). Symmetric, asymmetric, and hash types exist.
A security config where access is denied to any entity unless it appears on an allow list.
Network-based attack where the attacker dramatically increases bandwidth sent to a victim during a DDoS attack via an amplification factor.
Incident response process assessing indicators to determine validity, impact, and category.
Total annual cost of a risk = SLE × ARO.
Probability/likelihood of a risk expressed as times per year expected to occur.
Systems that detect users/hosts/services deviating from expectations, or training encouraging employee reporting of such deviations.
Inspecting traffic to locate and block viruses.
Software detecting/removing viruses and other malware (worms, Trojans, rootkits, adware, spyware, password crackers, network mappers, DoS tools, etc.).
Concept that most IT requirements can be deployed as a cloud service model.
A standalone hardware device performing only firewall functions.
Methods exposed by a script/program allowing other programs to use it.
Software delivery model where code runs on a server and is streamed to a client.
Vulnerability allowing an attacker to run their own code or exploit module.
Network attack redirecting an IP address to the MAC address of an unintended host; enables DoS, spoofing, on-path attacks.
Science of creating machines with problem-solving/analysis capability without significant human direction.
A thing of economic value; classified as tangible/intangible or short/long term.
Cipher using mathematically-linked public/private keys (RSA, ECC); private key not derivable from public key.
Points where a network/application receives external connections or I/O that could be exploited.
A specific path by which a threat actor gains unauthorized access to a system.
Capability of an authenticator/cryptographic module to prove it is a root of trust.
Access control technique evaluating a set of attributes each subject possesses.
Method of validating a particular entity's/individual's unique credentials.
Centralized platform verifying identity, assigning permissions, and logging actions for an audit trail.
IPSec protocol providing authentication, integrity, and replay protection for transmitted data.
A PNAC switch/router activating EAPoL and passing supplicant auth data to an authenticating server (e.g., RADIUS).
A hacker engaged in authorized penetration testing or security consultancy.
Process of determining what rights/privileges an entity has.
Security goal ensuring systems operate continuously and authorized persons can access needed data.
Mechanism for gaining computer access that bypasses normal authentication.
Security copy of production data made to removable media on a schedule (full, incremental, differential).
Standby power supply (diesel/propane) providing power after a UPS bridges the initial gap.
Security/config settings applied to a particular system/network.
Network monitoring detecting changes in normal operating sequences and identifying abnormal sequences.
Authentication using biometric scans (facial, iris, retina, fingerprint, signature).
Password attack exploiting encryption algorithm weaknesses via probability of collision.
Demanding payment to prevent release of information.
Security config permitting access generally except explicitly prohibited entities.
Expanding list of transactional records in a public ledger secured via cryptography.
Indicator of malicious activity: audit logs show unauthorized attempts to read/copy data.
Sending unsolicited messages/pictures via Bluetooth.
Wireless attack gaining unauthorized access to device info via Bluetooth.
Sturdy vertical posts controlling road traffic or preventing ram-raiding/vehicle-ramming.
Group of hosts/devices infected by a bot control program, enabling attackers to mount attacks.
Framework/tools facilitating personally owned device use for corporate access.
Password attack exhaustively trying every combination.
Attack where data exceeds destination buffer boundary, corrupting memory; can crash system or execute arbitrary code.
Reward scheme for reporting vulnerabilities.
Processes enabling normal operations during adverse events.
Impersonation attack using a compromised employee account to convince others to commit fraud.
Identifies organizational risks and their effect on mission-critical operations.
Agreement for two companies to work closely together (e.g., reseller/solution provider partnerships).
Physical theft protection using cable ties/padlocks; may include lockable faceplates.
Proxy server feature retaining copies of frequently requested web pages.
Document of authorized contacts for incident notification/collaboration.
Encoding input characters to evade input validation.
Estimating personnel/storage/hardware/software/connectivity resources needed over time.
Making a copy of a contactless access card.
Data access standards over cellular networks (2G/3G GSM/CDMA; 4G/5G under LTE).
Model where all data processing/storage occurs in a single location.
Validating a certificate by tracing signing CAs up to the root CA.
List of certificates revoked before expiration.
Base64 ASCII file a subject sends to a CA to obtain a certificate.
Third-party asset disposal technique using sanitization/destruction, with documentary evidence.
Record of evidence handling from collection through court to disposal.
Process by which the need for change is recorded/approved.
Process implementing configuration changes as part of overall config management.
Officer with primary responsibility for IT assets/procedures.
Person with overall responsibility for info assurance/systems security.
Officer responsible for effective use of new computing platforms/innovations.
Linux command for managing file permissions.
Provisioning model where employees select from corporate device options.
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — three principles of security control/management (also AIC).
Lists of cryptographic algorithms a server/client can use to negotiate a secure connection.
Enciphered data unreadable without the cipher key.
Policy mandating work areas free of sensitive documents.
Quickly duplicating a VM's configuration for identical machine deployment.
Software code/research remaining owned by the developer, used only under license.
On-demand architecture with high availability/scalability/elasticity, billed by metered usage.
Classifying cloud ownership/management: public, private, community, hybrid.
Classifying cloud service provision and CSP responsibility limits (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS, etc.).
Org providing infrastructure/application/storage "as a service."
Load balancing technique where servers work together as a unit.
Professional behavior standards based on ethics (honesty, fairness).
Using a digital signature to ensure source/integrity of programming code.
Predetermined alternate location for rebuilding a network after disaster.
Two different plaintext inputs producing the same ciphertext output.
Infrastructure attackers use to direct/distribute/control malware over botnets.
